Operative

Operative

Operatives fight the war no one sees, wearing borrowed faces, stealing secrets, and striking from the shadows.

Starting Evasion
12
Starting Hit Points
5
Class Items
A set of forged identity chips, or a coded message you've never cracked

Operative's Hope Feature

Gone to Ground: Spend 3 Hope to become Hidden, even while observed. Adversaries lose track of you until you move into their line of sight or make an attack.

Class Features

Covert Operative: When you make a roll to sneak, disguise yourself, gather intelligence, or bypass security, you can mark a Stress to roll with advantage.

Exploit Weakness: When you attack an adversary who is unaware of you or distracted, you gain a +2 bonus to the attack roll.

Operative Subclasses

Choose either the Spy or Assassin subclass.

SPY

Play the Spy if you want to become anyone and learn everything.

Spellcast Trait: Finesse

Foundation Feature

Deep Cover: After observing a person for several minutes, you can convincingly imitate their mannerisms and behavior. You have advantage on rolls to impersonate someone you've observed.

Specialization Feature

Perfect Cover: While impersonating someone you've observed, you can mark a Stress to reroll a failed roll to keep up the deception.

Mastery Feature

Many Faces: Once per session, you can reveal that you've been in the current scene all along, disguised as a minor character such as a guard, a servant, or a technician. With the GM's approval, step out of that disguise wherever that character stands.

ASSASSIN

Play the Assassin if you want to end a fight before your target knows it started.

Spellcast Trait: Finesse

Foundation Feature

Kill Shot: When you succeed with Hope on an attack against an adversary who is unaware of you, add a number of d8s equal to your tier to the damage roll.

Specialization Feature

Silent Kill: When you defeat an adversary who was unaware of you, other adversaries don't notice unless they can see the body, and you stay Hidden if you were.

Mastery Feature

Death Mark: Kill Shot adds d10s instead of d8s. Additionally, once per rest, you can use Kill Shot on a success with Fear.

Character Guide

Suggested Traits: Agility +1, Strength −1, Finesse +2, Instinct +1, Presence +0, Knowledge +0

Suggested Gear: DH-17 Blaster Pistol; Vibroknife; Flight Suit

Clothes: An officer's uniform that isn't yours, a dark hooded jacket, plain worker's coveralls, a long gray coat, a comlink earpiece

Personality: A chameleon, a spider, an accountant, a ghost, a locked box

Background Questions

  • Who recruited you, and do you still work for them?

  • What cover identity have you worn so long that you're afraid of forgetting who you really are?

  • What did you do in the line of duty that you can never take back?

Connections

  • How much of what I've told you about myself is true?

  • What secret of yours do I know?

  • Why did I choose you to watch my back?

Operative cards

21 cards, from level 1 to 10. Take two level 1 cards at creation, then one new card each time you level up, at your level or lower.

Level 1 Tier 1

Holo-Disguise

Level 1 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 0

A flicker of light, and you're wearing a stranger's face.

When you have a few minutes to prepare, you can mark a Stress to activate a holographic disguise and take on the appearance of any humanoid you can picture clearly in your mind. While disguised, you have advantage on Presence Rolls to avoid scrutiny.

Place a number of tokens equal to your Spellcast trait on this card. When you take an action while disguised, spend a token from this card. After the action that spends the last token is resolved, the disguise drops.

Infiltrator's Kit

Level 1 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 2

Shock gloves, a grapple line, and enough smoke to vanish in.

Shock Gloves: Make a Spellcast Roll against up to three adversaries within Melee range. Targets you succeed against take 2d6 physical damage and must mark a Stress as current arcs from your hands.

Grapple Line: Fire a cable to a point you can see within Far range. You can pull a small, unattended object to you, or pull yourself to that point.

Smoke Grenade: Make a Spellcast Roll (13) to fill a stationary area within Very Close range with temporary thick smoke. The smoke heavily obscures this area and everything in it.

Sabotage

Level 1 Operative Ability · Recall Cost: 1

A loose wire here, a stripped bolt there, and nobody will ever know.

Spend a Hope to secretly rig a weapon, vehicle, door, or machine within Melee range. The next time anyone uses it, it fails: an attack with it misses, a vehicle stalls, or a door won't open.

Level 2 Tier 2

Spy Kit

Level 2 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 2

A holo-mask, a targeting uplink, and a decoy that looks just like you.

Holo-Mask: You shift your appearance and clothing with a holographic mask to avoid recognition.

Tactical Uplink: Spend 2 Hope to link yourself or an ally within Close range to your targeting uplink. The next time the target makes an attack, they can hit an additional target within range that their attack roll would succeed against. You can only maintain the uplink on one creature at a time.

Holo-Decoy: Make a Spellcast Roll (14). On a success, project a temporary hologram no larger than you within Close range that lasts for as long as you look at it. It holds up to scrutiny until an observer is within Melee range.

Probe Droid

Level 2 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 1

A black sphere drifts out over the ridge, antennae twitching.

Spend a Hope to deploy a probe droid that can scout, move, or carry things for you until your next rest.

You can also send it at an adversary to self-destruct. When you do, make a Spellcast Roll against a target within Very Far range. On a success, the droid moves into Melee range with that target and explodes. Roll a number of d6s equal to your Spellcast trait and deal that much physical damage to the target. You can only have one probe droid at a time.

Level 3 Tier 2

Blackout

Level 3 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 1

You kill the lights. Your goggles switch to thermal.

Make a Spellcast Roll (13). On a success, you can create a temporary curtain of darkness, by cutting the power or deploying a blackout field, between two points within Far range. Only you can see through this darkness. You're considered Hidden to adversaries on the other side of it, and you have advantage on attacks you make through the darkness. The darkness remains until you use another Spell.

Spook's Kit

Level 3 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 2

Tools for making people float, forget, and fall down.

Grav Lift: Make a Spellcast Roll to temporarily lift a target you can see into the air with a repulsor field and move them within Close range of their original position.

Neural Scrambler: Spend a Hope to force a target within Melee range to make a Reaction Roll (15). On a failure, they forget the last minute of your conversation.

Shock Mine: Mark a Stress to drop a temporary shock mine where you stand. All adversaries within Melee range, or who enter Melee range, take 2d12+4 physical damage and are knocked back to Very Close range.

Level 4 Tier 2

Ghost Walk

Level 4 Operative Ability · Recall Cost: 0

Patrols walk right past you, and right past your team.

When you roll with Fear while attempting to move unnoticed through a dangerous area, you can mark a Stress to roll with Hope instead.

If an ally within Close range is also attempting to move unnoticed and rolls with Fear, you can mark a Stress to change their result to a roll with Hope.

Countermeasures Kit

Level 4 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 2

Every exit covered, every threat accounted for.

Deflector Pulse: Once per long rest, spend a Hope to negate the damage of an attack targeting you or an ally within Very Close range.

Mag-Clamp: Target an object within Far range. That object locks in place exactly where it is until your next rest. If a creature tries to move it, make a Spellcast Roll against them to keep it locked.

Laser Tripwire: Make a Spellcast Roll (15). On a success, create a fence of laser tripwires between two points within Far range. All creatures in its path must choose a side to be on, and anything that subsequently passes through the fence takes 4d10+3 physical damage.

Level 5 Tier 3

Dead Zone

Level 5 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 1

No alarms, no comms, no screams.

Make a Spellcast Roll against a target within Close range. On a success, spend a Hope to project a dampening field around the target that encompasses everything within Very Close range of them and follows them as they move.

The target and anything within the area is Silenced until the GM spends a Fear on their turn to clear this condition, you use Dead Zone again, or you take Major damage. While Silenced, they can't make noise and can't call for help or reinforcements.

Exfil Beacon

Level 5 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 2

There's always a way out, if you planned it in advance.

Spend a Hope to plant an exfil beacon where you're currently standing. Spend another Hope at any time before your next rest to slip away from where you are and reappear at the beacon, then describe the escape route you planned. This effect ends after you reappear.

Level 6 Tier 3

Team Disguise

Level 6 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 0

Matching uniforms, forged faces, and one shared cover story.

When you have a few minutes of silence to focus, you can mark a Stress to change the appearance of all willing creatures within Close range with holo-disguises. Their new forms must share a general body structure and size, and can be somebody you've seen before or entirely fabricated. A disguised creature has advantage on Presence Rolls to avoid scrutiny.

Activate a Countdown (8). It ticks down as a consequence the GM chooses. When it triggers, the disguises drop.

Handler Link

Level 6 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 0

A covert earpiece and a contact who never stops listening.

You can speak to any person you've made physical contact with, through a covert comm you planted on them. Once you've opened a channel with them, they can speak back to you.

Additionally, you can mark a Stress to make a Spellcast Roll against them. On a success, you can ask the GM one of the following questions and receive an answer:

  • Where are they?

  • What are they doing?

  • What are they afraid of?

  • What do they cherish most in the world?

Level 7 Tier 3

Fade Out

Level 7 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 1

The shot misses, and you're already somewhere else.

When an attack made against you that would deal physical damage fails, you can spend a Hope to vanish into the shadows, becoming Hidden and moving to a point within Close range of the attacker. You remain Hidden until the next time you make an action roll.

Insertion Kit

Level 7 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 0

Through the wall and past the checkpoint without a trace.

Phase Cutter: Make a Spellcast Roll (13). Once per rest on a success, you and all creatures touching you pass through a wall or door within Close range. The opening seals behind you once everyone is through.

Forged Clearance: Make a Spellcast Roll (14). Once per long rest on a success, forged credentials get you and your allies past a checkpoint and into a secure facility you know of. The credentials hold until your next rest.

Level 8 Tier 4

Shadow Operative

Level 8 Operative Ability · Recall Cost: 2

In the dark, you're the most dangerous thing in the room.

While you're in low light or darkness, you gain a +1 bonus to your Evasion and make attack rolls with advantage.

Interrogation Kit

Level 8 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 2

Nobody keeps a secret from you for long.

Mind Probe: Make a Spellcast Roll against a target within Close range. On a success, probe the target's mind and ask the GM a question. The GM describes any memories the target has pertaining to the answer.

Encrypted Link: Once per long rest, spend a Hope to choose two willing creatures. When one of them would mark Stress, they can choose between the two of them who marks it. This link lasts until their next rest.

Level 9 Tier 4

Deep Cover Kit

Level 9 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 4

Become part of the scenery, then take everything they have.

Object Mimicry: Make a Spellcast Roll (15). On a success, a holo-camouflage field disguises you as an inanimate object no larger than twice your normal size. You can remain in this shape until you take damage.

Total Compromise: Once per long rest, make a Spellcast Roll against a target within Close range. On a success, you've exposed every weakness they have, and they become permanently Vulnerable. They can't clear this condition by any means.

Long Game

Level 9 Operative Ability · Recall Cost: 1

Every piece of intel you gather sharpens the final blow.

Choose a target within Far range. When you succeed on an action roll against them that doesn't result in making a damage roll, place a token on this card. When you deal damage to this target, spend any number of tokens to add a d12 for each token spent to your damage roll. You can only play the Long Game against one creature at a time.

When you choose a new target or take a rest, clear all unspent tokens.

Level 10 Tier 4

Lights Out

Level 10 Operative Spell · Recall Cost: 2

Every light in the facility dies at once.

Make a Spellcast Roll (16). Once per long rest on a success, plunge the entire area within Far range into complete darkness that only you and your allies can see through. Attack rolls have disadvantage when targeting you or an ally within this darkness.

Additionally, when you or an ally succeeds with Hope against an adversary within this darkness, the target must mark a Stress.

This effect lasts until the GM spends a Fear on their turn to clear it or you take Severe damage.

Masterstroke Kit

Level 10 Operative Grimoire · Recall Cost: 2

The perfect ambush, and a field even the Force can't touch.

Perfect Ambush: Make a Spellcast Roll (18). On a success, everyone within Far range except you is caught completely off guard and can't act. This lasts until the next time you make an action roll that targets another creature.

Force Dampener: Spend 5 Hope to activate a Force-dampening field around yourself and become immune to magic damage until your next rest.

Chapter 4

Core Mechanics

Core Mechanics

Kyberheart uses the Daggerheart SRD's core mechanics without change: the flow of the game, the spotlight, action and reaction rolls, Hope and Fear, advantage and disadvantage, Help an Ally, Tag Team Rolls, Group Action Rolls, combat and attacking, damage thresholds and Armor Slots, Stress, range and movement, the standard conditions (Hidden, Restrained, and Vulnerable), downtime, death moves, and scars. Those unchanged Daggerheart rules are included below, each marked with a gold tag, alongside what Kyberheart changes. Rules unique to Kyberheart are in Kyberheart Mechanics.

Flow of the Game

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

Kyberheart is a conversation. The GM describes fictional scenarios involving the PCs, and the players take turns describing how their characters react. The goal of every person at the table is to build upon everyone else’s ideas and collaboratively tell a satisfying story. The system facilitates this collaborative process by providing structure to the conversation and mechanics for resolving moments of tension where fate or fortune determine the outcome of events.

Player Principles & Best Practices

To get the most out of Kyberheart, we recommend players keep the following principles and practices in mind throughout each session:

Principles

  • Be a fan of your character and their journey.

  • Spotlight your friends.

  • Address the characters and address the players.

  • Build the world together.

  • Play to find out what happens.

  • Hold on gently.

Best Practices

  • Embrace danger.

  • Use your resources.

  • Tell the story.

  • Discover your character.

Core Gameplay Loop

The core gameplay loop is the procedure that drives every scene, both in and out of combat:

Step 1: Set the Scene

The GM describes a scenario, establishing the PCs’ surroundings and any dangers, NPCs, or other important details the characters would notice.

Step 2: Ask and Answer Questions

The players ask clarifying questions to explore the scene more deeply and gather information that could inform their characters’ actions. The GM responds to these questions by giving the players information their characters could easily obtain, or by asking questions of their own to the players. The players also respond to any questions the GM poses to them. In this way, the table builds out the fiction collaboratively.

Step 3: Build on the Fiction

As the scene develops, the players find opportunities to take action—problems to solve, obstacles to overcome, mysteries to investigate, and so on. The players describe how their characters proceed; if their proposed actions carry no chance of failure (or if failure would be boring), they automatically succeed. But if the outcome of their action is unknown, the GM calls for an action roll. Either way, the table works the outcome into the story and moves the fiction forward, narrating how the PC’s actions have changed things.

Step 4: Go Back to Step 1

The process repeats from the beginning, with the GM relaying any updated details or material changes to the players. This process continues until the end of the scene is triggered by a mechanic or arrives organically.

The Spotlight

The spotlight is a symbol that represents the table’s attention—and therefore the immediate focus of both the narrative and the game mechanics. Any time a character or player becomes the focus of a scene, they “are in the spotlight” or “have the spotlight.” The spotlight moves around the table organically as scenes unfold unless a mechanical trigger determines where the spotlight goes next. For example, when a player fails an action roll, the mechanics prompt the GM to seize the spotlight and make a GM move.

Turn Order & Action Economy

Kyberheart’s turns don’t follow a traditional, rigid format: there is no explicit initiative mechanic and characters don’t have a set number of actions they can take or things they can do before the spotlight passes to someone else. A player with the spotlight describes what their character does and the spotlight simply swings to whoever:

  1. the fiction would naturally turn it toward

  2. hasn’t had the focus in a while, or

  3. a triggered mechanic puts it on

Optional: Spotlight Tracker Tool

If your group prefers a more traditional action economy, you can use tokens to track how many times a player has had the spotlight: At the start of a session or scene, each player adds a certain number of tokens (we recommend 3) to their character sheet and removes a token each time they take an action. If the spotlight would swing to someone without any tokens, it swings to someone else instead. Once every player has used all their available tokens, players refill their character sheet with the same number of tokens as before, then continue playing.

Making Moves & Taking Action

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

Any time a character does something to advance the story, such as speaking with another character, interacting with the environment, making an attack, casting a spell, or using a class feature, they are making a move.

Action Rolls

Any move where success would be trivial or failure would be boring automatically succeeds, but any move that’s difficult to accomplish or risky to attempt triggers an action roll.

Overview

All action rolls require a pair of d12s called Duality Dice. These are two visually distinct twelve-sided dice, with one die representing Hope and the other representing Fear.

To make an action roll, you roll the Duality Dice, sum the results, apply any relevant modifiers, and compare the total to a Difficulty number to determine the outcome:

  • Success with Hope: If your total meets or beats the Difficulty AND your Hope Die shows a higher result than your Fear Die, you rolled a “Success with Hope.” You succeed and gain a Hope.

  • Success with Fear: If your total meets or beats the Difficulty AND your Fear Die shows a higher result than your Hope Die, you rolled a “Success with Fear.” You succeed with a cost or complication, but the GM gains a Fear.

  • Failure with Hope: If your total is less than the Difficulty AND your Hope Die shows a higher result than your Fear Die, you rolled a “Failure with Hope.” You fail with a minor consequence and gain a Hope, then the spotlight swings to the GM.

  • Failure with Fear: If your total is less than the Difficulty AND your Fear Die shows a higher result than your Hope Die, you rolled a “Failure with Fear.” You fail with a major consequence and the GM gains a Fear, then the spotlight swings to the GM.

  • Critical Success: If the Duality Dice show matching results, you rolled a “Critical Success” (“Crit”). You automatically succeed with a bonus, gain a Hope, and clear a Stress. If this was an attack roll, you deal critical damage. Note: A Critical Success counts as a roll “with Hope.”

After resolving the action roll, the table works together to weave the outcome into the narrative and play continues.

Failing Forward

In Kyberheart, every time you roll the dice, the scene changes in some way. There is no such thing as a roll where “nothing happens,” because the fiction constantly evolves based on the successes and failures of the characters.

Procedure

The following steps describe in more detail the procedure that all action rolls utilize:

Step 1: Pick An Appropriate Trait

Some actions and effects specify in their description which trait applies to the roll; otherwise, the GM tells the acting player which character trait best applies to the action being attempted. If more than one trait could apply to the roll, the GM chooses or lets the acting player decide.

Step 2: Determine the Difficulty

Some actions and features say in their description what the Difficulty is. Otherwise, the GM determines the Difficulty based on the scenario. The GM can choose whether to share the Difficulty with the table. In either case, the GM should communicate the potential consequences of failure to the acting player.

Step 3: Apply Extra Dice and Modifiers

The acting player decides whether to Utilize an Experience or activate other effects, then, if applicable, adds the appropriate tokens and dice (such as advantage or Rally dice) to their dice pool. Note: Unless an action, ability, or feature specifically allows for it, a player must declare the use of any Experiences, extra dice, or other modifiers before they roll.

Step 4: Roll the Dice

The acting player rolls their entire dice pool and announces the results in the format of “[total result] with [Hope/Fear]”—

or “Critical Success!” in the case of matching Duality Dice. Example: A player is making an action roll with a +1 in the relevant trait and no other modifiers; they roll the Duality Dice and get a result of 5 on their Hope Die and 7 on their Fear Die, then announce “I rolled a 13 with Fear!”

Step 5: Resolve the Outcome

The active player and the GM work together, along with the suggestions and support of the rest of the table, to resolve the outcome of the action.

GM Moves and Adversary Actions

GMs also make moves. They should consider making a move when a player does one of the following things:

  • Rolls with Fear on an action roll.

  • Fails an action roll.

  • Does something that would have consequences.

  • Gives them a golden opportunity.

  • Looks to them for what happens next.

After the GM turn is done, the spotlight goes back to the PCs.

Many adversaries and environments have Fear Features, especially powerful or consequential moves that the GM must spend Fear to activate.

Note: This Fear is in addition to any Fear the GM has previously spent to seize the spotlight or activate another action or ability.

Adversary Actions

When play passes to the GM, the GM can make a GM move to spotlight an adversary. A spotlighted adversary can:

  • Move within Close range and make a standard attack

  • Move within Close range and use an adversary action

  • Clear a condition

  • Sprint within Far or Very Far range on the battlefield

  • Do anything else the fiction demands or the GM deems appropriate

The GM can spend additional Fear to spotlight additional adversaries. Once the GM has finished, the spotlight swings back to the PCs.

Special Rolls

Some rolls have unique specifications or otherwise modify the action roll procedure: trait rolls, Spellcast Rolls, attack rolls, and damage rolls. Unless otherwise noted, you can apply any bonus, modifier, or effect to a special roll as if it were a standard action roll.

Trait Rolls

An action roll that specifies which character trait applies to it is called a trait roll. In the text of a feature or effect, a trait roll is referenced with the format “[Trait] Roll (Difficulty)” (e.g., “Agility Roll (12)”). If the text of an effect doesn’t specify a trait roll’s Difficulty, the GM sets the Difficulty based on the circumstances.

Features and effects that affect a trait roll also affect any action roll that uses the same trait, including attack rolls, Spellcast rolls, and standard action rolls. Example: The katari’s ancestry feature “Feline Instincts,” which allows the katari to reroll an Agility Roll, can also be used on a standard action roll using Agility to traverse dangerous terrain or on an attack roll made with a weapon that uses Agility.

Spellcast Rolls

Spellcast Rolls are trait rolls that require you to use your Spellcast trait. Your Spellcast trait, if you have one, is determined by your subclass.

Spellcast Rolls are only made when a character uses a feature that requires one. A successful Spellcast Roll activates the effect as described by the feature. Notes:

A Spellcast Roll that can damage a target is also considered an attack roll.

When you cast a spell, the text tells you when the effect ends. The GM can spend a Fear to end a temporary effect. If your spell doesn’t specify when it ends, it ends when you choose or at a natural moment of the story. You can choose to end your spell early.

You can cast and maintain the effects of more than one spell at the same time.

Reaction Rolls

A reaction roll is made in response to an attack or a hazard, representing a character’s attempt to avoid or withstand an imminent effect.

Reaction rolls work like action rolls, except they don’t generate Hope or Fear, don’t trigger additional GM moves, and other characters can’t aid you with Help an Ally.

If you critically succeed on a reaction roll, you don’t clear a Stress or gain a Hope, but you do ignore any effects that would have impacted you on a success, such as taking damage or marking Stress.

Group Action Rolls

When multiple PCs take action together, the party chooses one PC to lead the action. Each other player then describes how their character collaborates on the task. The leader makes an action roll as usual, while the other players make reaction rolls using whichever traits they and the GM decide fit best.

The lead character gains a +1 bonus to their lead action roll for each of these reaction rolls that succeeded and a −1 penalty for each these reaction rolls that failed.

Tag Team Rolls

Each player can, once per session, initiate a Tag Team Roll between their character and another PC by spending 3 Hope. The players work with one another to describe how they combine their actions in a unique and exciting way. Both players make separate action rolls; before resolving the roll’s outcome, choose one of the rolls to apply to both actions. On a roll with Hope, all PCs involved gain a Hope. On a roll with Fear, the GM gains a Fear token for each PC involved. On a successful Tag Team attack roll, both players roll damage and add the totals together to determine the damage dealt, which is then treated as if it came from a single source. If the attacks deal different types of damage, the players choose which type to deal.

Notes:

A Tag Team Roll counts as a single action roll for the purposes of any countdowns or features that track action rolls.

Though each player may only initiate one Tag Team Roll per session, one PC can be involved in multiple Tag Team Rolls.

Advantage & Disadvantage

Some features and effects let you roll with advantage or disadvantage on an action or reaction roll:

  • Advantage represents an opportunity that you seize to increase your chances of success. When you roll with advantage, you roll a d6 advantage die with your dice pool and add its result to your total.

  • Disadvantage represents an additional difficulty, hardship, or challenge you face when attempting an action. When you roll with disadvantage, you roll a d6 disadvantage die with your dice pool and subtract its result from your total.

Advantage or disadvantage can be granted or imposed by mechanical triggers or at the GM’s discretion. When a PC aids you with Help an Ally, they roll their own advantage die and you add it to your total.

Advantage and disadvantage dice cancel each out, one-forone, when they would be added to the same dice pool, so you’ll never roll both at the same time. If you have advantage or disadvantage from other sources that don’t affect your own dice pool, such as another player’s Help an Ally move, their effects stack with your rolled results.

Hope & Fear

Hope and Fear are metacurrencies representing the cosmic forces that shape the events of your table’s story. Hope powers PC abilities and features, while Fear powers the abilities of the GM and the adversaries and environments they control.

Hope

Every PC starts with 2 Hope at character creation and gains more throughout play. A PC can have a maximum of 6 Hope at one time, and Hope carries over between sessions.

Players can spend Hope to:

  • Help an Ally

When you Help an Ally who is making an action roll, describe how you do so and roll an advantage die. Multiple players can spend Hope to help the same acting player, but that player only adds the highest result to their final total.

  • Utilize an Experience

When you Utilize an Experience on a relevant roll, add its modifier to the result. You can spend multiple Hope to utilize multiple Experiences.

  • Initiate a Tag Team Roll

Spend 3 Hope to initiate a Tag Team roll, combining the actions of two PCs into one impressive act of synergy. When you make a Tag Team roll, both players roll their action rolls and then choose which set of results to apply to the outcome.

  • Activate a Hope Feature A Hope Feature is any effect that allows (or requires) you to spend a specified amount of Hope to activate it. Class Hope features are class-specific features, detailed on your character sheet, that cost 3 Hope to activate. Note: When using a Hope Feature, if you rolled with Hope for that action, the Hope you gain from that roll can be spent on that feature (or toward it, if it requires spending multiple Hope).

Fear

The GM gains Fear whenever a player rolls with Fear and can spend Fear at any time to make or enhance a GM move or to use a Fear Feature. The GM can have up to 12 Fear at one time. Fear carries over between sessions.

Combat

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

Though Kyberheart relies on the same flow of collaborative storytelling in and out of combat, physical conflicts rely more heavily on several key mechanics related to attacking, maneuvering, and taking damage.

Evasion

Evasion represents a character’s ability to avoid attacks and other unwanted effects. Any roll made against a PC has a Difficulty equal to the target’s Evasion. A PC’s base Evasion is determined by their class, but can be modified by class cards, equipment, conditions, and other effects. Note: attacks rolled against adversaries use the target’s Difficulty instead of Evasion.

Hit Points & Damage Thresholds

Hit Points (HP) represent a character’s ability to withstand physical injury. When a character takes damage, they mark 1 to 3 HP, based on their damage thresholds:

  • If the final damage is at or above the character’s Severe damage threshold, they mark 3 HP.

  • If the final damage is at or above the character’s Major damage threshold but below their Severe damage threshold, they mark 2 HP.

  • If the final damage is below the character’s Major damage threshold, they mark 1 HP.

  • If incoming damage is ever reduced to 0 or less, no HP is marked. A PC’s damage thresholds are calculated by adding their level to the listed damage thresholds of their equipped armor. A PC’s starting HP is based on their class, but they can gain additional Hit Points through advancements, features, and other effects.

An adversary’s Damage Thresholds and HP are listed in their stat blocks.

When a character marks their last Hit Point, they fall. If a PC falls, they make a death move.

Characters can clear Hit Points by taking downtime moves (see: Downtime) or by activating relevant special abilities or effects.

Optional Rule: Massive Damage

If a character ever takes damage equal to twice their Severe threshold, they mark 4 HP instead of 3.

Stress

Stress represents how much mental, physical, and emotional strain a character can endure. Some special abilities or effects require the character activating them to mark Stress, and the GM can require a PC to mark Stress as a GM move or to represent the cost, complication, or consequence of an action roll. When a character marks their last Stress, they become Vulnerable (see: Conditions) until they clear at least 1 Stress. When a character must mark 1 or more Stress but can’t, they mark 1 HP instead. A character can’t use a move that requires them to mark Stress if all of their Stress is marked. PCs can clear Stress by making downtime moves (see: Downtime). A PC’s maximum Stress is determined by their class, but they can increase it through advancements, abilities, and other effects.

Attacking

Attack Rolls

An attack roll is an action roll intended to inflict harm. The trait that applies to an attack roll is specified by the weapon or spell being used. Unarmed attack rolls use either Strength or Finesse (GM’s choice). An attack roll’s Difficulty, unless otherwise noted, is equal to the Difficulty score of its target.

Damage Rolls

On a successful attack, roll damage. Damage is calculated from the damage roll listed in the attack’s description with the format “xdy+[modifier]” (e.g., for a spell that inflicts “1d8+2” damage, you roll an eight-sided and add 2 to the result; the damage dealt is equal to the total).

Any time an effect says to deal damage using your Spellcast trait, you roll a number of dice equal to your Spellcast trait. Note: If your Spellcast trait is +0 or lower, you don’t roll anything.

For weapons, the number of damage dice you roll is equal to your Proficiency. Note that your Proficiency multiplies the number of dice you roll, but doesn’t affect the modifier. For example, a PC with Proficiency 2 and wielding a weapon with a damage rating of “d8+2” deals damage equal to “2d8+2” on a successful attack. Successful unarmed attacks inflict [Proficiency]d4 damage.

Critical Damage

When you get a critical success (i.e., you roll matching values on your Duality Dice) on an attack roll, you deal extra damage. Make the damage roll as usual, but add the maximum possible result of the damage dice to the final total. For instance, if an attack would normally deal 2d8+1 damage, a critical success would deal 2d8+1+16.

Resistance, Immunity, and Direct Damage

If a target has resistance to a damage type, then they reduce incoming damage of that type by half before comparing it to their Hit Point Thresholds. If the target has additional ways of reducing incoming damage, such as marking Armor Slots, they apply the resistance effect first. The effects of multiple resistances to the same damage type do not stack.

If a target has immunity to a damage type, they ignore incoming damage of that type.

If an attack deals both physical and magic damage, a character can only benefit from resistance or immunity if they are resistant or immune to both damage types.

Direct damage is damage that can’t be reduced by marking Armor Slots.

Multi-target Attack Rolls

If a spell or ability allows you to target multiple adversaries, make one attack roll and one damage roll, then apply the results to each target individually.

Multiple Damage Sources

Damage dealt simultaneously from multiple sources is always totaled before it’s compared to its target’s damage thresholds. For example, if a PC with Wookiee ancestry makes a successful attack against a target in Melee range and decides to spend a Hope to use their “Tusks” feature (which gives them an extra 1d6 damage on a damage roll), they would roll their normal weapon damage and add a d6 to the result, then deal that total damage to the adversary.

Maps, Range, and Movement

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

You can play Kyberheart using “theater of the mind” or maps and miniatures. The conversions below from abstract ranges to physical measurements assume 1 inch of map represents about 5 feet of fictional space.

Kyberheart uses the following ranges to translate fictional positioning into relative distance for the purposes of targeting, movement, and other game mechanics:

Melee: Close enough to touch, up to a few feet away.

Very Close: Close enough to see fine details, about 5–10 feet away. While in danger, a character can move, as part of their action, from Very Close range into Melee range. On a map: anything within the shortest length of a game card (2-3 inches).

Close: Close enough to see prominent details, about 10–30 feet away. While in danger, a character can move, as part of their action, from Close range into Melee range. On a map: anything within the length of a pencil (5-6 inches).

Far: Close enough to see very little detail, about 30–100 feet away. While in danger, a character must make an Agility Roll to safely move from Far range into Melee range. On a map: anything within the length of the long edge of a piece of copy paper (11–12 inches).

Very Far: Too far to make out any details, about 100–300 feet away. While in danger, a character must make an Agility Roll to safely move from Very Far range into Melee range. On a map: anything beyond Far range, but still within the bounds of the conflict or scene.

Out of Range: Anything beyond a character’s Very Far range is Out of Range and usually can’t be targeted.

Range is measured from the source of an effect, such as the attacker or spellcaster, to the target or object of an effect.

A weapon, spell, ability, item, or other effect’s stated range is a maximum range; unless otherwise noted, it can be used at closer distances.

Optional Rule: Defined Ranges

If your table would rather operate with more precise range rules, you can use a 1-inch grid battle map during combat. If you do, use the following guidelines for play:

  • Melee: 1 square

  • Very Close: 3 squares

  • Close: 6 squares

  • Far: 12 squares

  • Very Far: 13+ squares

  • Out of Range: Off the battlemap

Movement Under Pressure

When you’re under pressure or in danger and make an action roll, you can move to a location within Close range as part of that action. If you’re not already making an action roll, or if you want to move farther than your Close range, you need to succeed on an Agility Roll to safely reposition yourself.

An adversary can move within Close range for free as part of an action, or within Very Far range as a separate action.

Area of Effect

Unless stated otherwise, all the targets of a group effect must be within Very Close range of a single origin point within your effect’s range.

Line of Sight & Cover

Unless stated otherwise, a ranged attacker must have line of sight to their intended target to make an attack roll. If a partial obstruction lies between the attacker and target, the target has cover. Attacks made through cover are rolled with disadvantage. If the obstruction is total, there is no line of sight.

Conditions

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

Conditions are effects that grant specific benefits or drawbacks to the target they are attached to.

Standard Conditions

Kyberheart has three standard conditions:

Hidden

While you’re out of sight from all enemies and they don’t otherwise know your location, you gain the Hidden

condition. Any rolls against a Hidden creature have disadvantage. After an adversary moves to where they would see you, you move into their line of sight, or you make an attack, you are no longer Hidden.

Restrained

Restrained characters can’t move, but you can still take actions from their current position.

Vulnerable

When a creature is Vulnerable, all rolls targeting them have advantage. Some features can apply special or unique conditions, which work as described in the feature text.

Unless otherwise noted, the same condition can’t be applied more than once to the same target.

Temporary Tags & Special Conditions

The temporary tag denotes a condition or effect that the affected creature can clear by making a move against it. When an affected PC makes a move to clear a temporary condition or effect, it normally requires a successful action roll using an appropriate trait. When an affected adversary makes a move to clear a temporary condition or effect, the GM puts the spotlight on the adversary and describes how they do it; this doesn’t require a roll but it does use up that adversary’s spotlight.

Special conditions are only cleared when specific requirements are met, such as completing a certain action or using a particular item. The requirements for clearing these conditions are stated in the text of the effect that applies the condition.

Downtime

Resting and Downtime Moves

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

Between conflicts, the party can take a rest to recover expended resources and deepen their bonds. During a rest, each PC can make up to two downtime moves.

When the party rests, they must choose between a short rest and a long rest. If a party takes three short rests in a row, their next rest must be a long rest.

If a short rest is interrupted, such as by an adversary's attack, the characters don’t gain its benefits. If a long rest is interrupted, the characters only gain the benefits of a short rest. A short rest lasts enough time for the party to catch its breath, about an hour in-world. Each player can move class cards between their loadout and vault for free, then choose twice from the following list of downtime moves (players can choose the same move twice):

  • Tend to Wounds: Clear 1d4+Tier Hit Points for yourself or an ally.

  • Clear Stress: Clear 1d4+Tier Stress.

  • Repair Armor: Clear 1d4+Tier Armor Slots from your or an ally’s armor.

  • Prepare: Describe how you prepare yourself for the path ahead, then gain a Hope. If you choose to Prepare with one or more members of your party, you each gain 2 Hope.

At the end of a short rest, any features or effects with a limited number of uses per rest refresh and any features or effects that last until your next rest expire. A long rest is when the characters make camp and relax or sleep for several in-game hours. Each player can move class cards between their loadout and vault for free, then choose twice from the following list of downtime moves (players can choose the same move twice):

  • Tend to All Wounds: Clear all Hit Points for yourself or an ally.

  • Clear All Stress: Clear all Stress.

  • Repair All Armor: Clear all Armor Slots from your or an ally’s armor

  • Prepare: Describe how you prepare for the next day’s adventure, then gain a Hope. If you choose to Prepare with one or more members of your party, you each gain 2 Hope.

  • Work on a Project: With GM approval, a PC may pursue a long-term project, such as deciphering an ancient text or crafting a new weapon. The first time they start a new project, assign it a countdown. Each time a PC makes the Work on a Project move, they either advance their project’s countdown automatically or make an action roll to advance it (GM’s choice).

At the end of a long rest, any features or effects with a limited number of uses per rest or per long rest refresh and any features or effects that last until your next rest or until your next long rest expire.

Downtime Consequences

On a short rest, the GM gains 1d4 Fear. On a long rest, they gain Fear equal to 1d4 + the number of PCs, and they can advance a long-term countdown of their choice.

Kyberheart keeps the Daggerheart SRD's downtime moves (Tend to Wounds, Clear Stress, Repair Armor, Prepare, and Work on a Project) and adds these:

Downtime moveRestEffect
Repair DroidShort or longWith a Tool Kit, clear 1d4 Stress on a droid companion. If it was Offline, it comes back online.
Patch UpShortWith a Tool Kit, clear 1d4 + your tier in ship Stress and Shield Slots, in any combination, or fix one Critical System.
OverhaulLongWith a Tool Kit, clear all ship Stress and Shield Slots, fix all Critical Systems, and clear 1d4 Hull.
CraftShort or longWith a loot formula and its components, craft the consumable it lists.

Projects During Downtime

The Work on a Project downtime move lets a PC pursue a long-term goal, as in the Daggerheart SRD. With GM approval, the first time a PC starts a project, the GM assigns it a progress countdown. Each time the PC takes Work on a Project, the countdown advances automatically for a simple project; a complex project requires an action roll.

When setting a countdown, consider how complex the project is, whether the PC has the right tools and help, and how much it will change the story. A Tool Kit, a Slicer Kit, a workshop, or a knowledgeable ally can lower a countdown by 1. For complex projects, use the same progress table as attuning a kyber crystal: tick down 2 on a success with Hope, 1 on a success with Fear, and none on a failure.

Example Projects

ProjectCountdownRoll (complex only)Result
Attune a kyber crystal or build a lightsaberSee Kyber Crystals and LightsabersSee Kyber Crystals and LightsabersAn attuned crystal or a new lightsaber
Forge Imperial IDs for the crew3SimpleSame as buying New Identities: clear 2 Imperial Heat

Pay off a debt to a crime lord4Simple, plus the credits owedThe debt is settled and the bounty is lifted
Decrypt stolen Imperial data4Knowledge (14)Learn one secret the data holds, such as a shipment, a name, or a weak point
Scout an Imperial garrison3Instinct (13)Learn the patrol routes: advantage on your first roll in that location's environment
Restore a droid's wiped memory3Knowledge (13)The droid recovers a memory, and the GM reveals a secret it saw
Open a Jedi or Sith holocron5Spellcast (16), Force Adepts onlyLearn a lost teaching or secret; opening a Sith holocron gives a Darkness token in The Dark Times

Extended Downtime

When the story jumps ahead weeks or months, use montages to show the passage of time. As in the Daggerheart SRD, the GM gains 1d6 Fear per PC and advances any long-term countdowns as appropriate, including projects. In The Dark Times, extended downtime also clears 1 Imperial Heat.

Death

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

When a PC marks their last Hit Point, they must make a death move by choosing one of the following options:

  • Blaze of Glory: Your character embraces death and goes out in a blaze of glory. Take one final action. It automatically critically succeeds (with GM approval), and then you cross through the veil of death.

  • Avoid Death: Your character avoids death and faces the consequences. They temporarily drop unconscious, and then you work with the GM to describe how the situation worsens. While unconscious, your character can’t move or act, and they can’t be targeted by an attack. They return to consciousness when an ally clears 1 or more of their marked Hit Points or when the party finishes a long rest. After your character falls unconscious, roll your Hope Die. If its value is equal to or less than your character’s level, they gain a scar: permanently cross out a Hope slot and work with the GM to determine its lasting narrative impact and how, if possible, it can be restored. If you ever cross out your last Hope slot, your character’s journey ends.

  • Risk It All: Roll your Duality Dice. If the Hope Die is higher, your character stays on their feet and clears a number of Hit Points or Stress equal to the value of the Hope Die (you can divide the Hope Die value between Hit Points and Stress however you’d prefer). If the Fear Die is higher, your character crosses through the veil of death. If the Duality Dice show matching results, your character stays up and clears all Hit Points and Stress.

If your character dies, work with the GM before the next session to create a new character at the current level of the rest of the party.

Additional Rules

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

The following rules apply to many aspects of the game.

Rounding Up

This game doesn’t use fractions; if you need to round to a whole number, round up unless otherwise specified. When in doubt, resolve any ambiguity in favor of the PCs.

Rerolling Dice

When a feature allows you to reroll a die, you always take the new result unless the feature specifically says otherwise.

Incoming Damage

Incoming damage means the total damage from a single attack or source, before Armor Slots are marked.

Simultaneous Effects

If the resolution order of multiple effects is unclear, the person in control of the effects (player or GM) decides what order to resolve them in.

Stacking Effects

Unless stated otherwise, all effects beside conditions and advantage/disadvantage can stack.

Ongoing Spell Effects

If an effect doesn’t have a listed mechanical expiration, it only ends when decided by the controlling player, the GM, or the demands of the fiction.

Spending Resources

Unless an effect states otherwise, you can’t spend Hope or mark Stress multiple times on the same feature to increase or repeat its effects on the same roll.

Using Features After a Roll

If a feature allows you to affect a roll after the result has been totaled, you can use it after the GM declares whether the roll succeeds or fails, but not after the consequences unfold or another roll is made.

Credits

Kyberheart uses Daggerheart's gold rules unchanged, renamed as credits: 10 handfuls make a bag, and 10 bags make a chest. See the Equipment chapter for prices and payouts.

Leveling Up

Your party levels up whenever the GM decides you've reached a narrative milestone, usually about every three sessions. All party members level up at the same time.

TierLevels
Tier 1Level 1
Tier 2Levels 2–4
Tier 3Levels 5–7
Tier 4Levels 8–10

Step One: Tier Achievements

  • Level 2: Gain a new Experience at +2 and permanently increase your Proficiency by 1.

  • Level 5: Gain a new Experience at +2, permanently increase your Proficiency by 1, and clear any marked traits.

  • Level 8: Gain a new Experience at +2, permanently increase your Proficiency by 1, and clear any marked traits.

Step Two: Advancements

Choose two advancements with an unmarked slot from your tier or below, as in the Daggerheart SRD: increase two unmarked traits, add a Hit Point slot, add a Stress slot, increase an Experience, take an additional class card, increase your Evasion, take an upgraded subclass card (Tiers 3 and 4), increase your Proficiency (two advancements), or multiclass (two advancements, Tiers 3 and 4).

When an advancement mentions a domain card, use a class card from your class's deck instead.

Step Three: Damage Thresholds

Increase all your damage thresholds by 1.

Step Four: Class Cards

Take a new class card at your level or lower from your class's deck, and add it to your loadout or vault. You can also exchange one class card you already have for a different card of the same level or lower.

Multiclassing

Starting at level 5, you can choose multiclassing as an option when leveling up. It uses the multiclass advancement in Tiers 3 and 4, which costs two advancements. When you multiclass:

  • Choose a second class. Gain one of its class features. If it has more than one, choose which.

  • Take a foundation. Take the foundation features of one of its subclasses. If your foundations specify different Spellcast traits, you can choose which one to use each time you make a Spellcast Roll.

  • Gain access to its deck. Whenever you can acquire a new class card, you can choose from cards at or below half your current level (rounded up) from the second class's deck.

  • Keep your core. You don't gain the second class's Hope Feature, starting Evasion, starting Hit Points, or class items.

  • Cross out options. Cross out the upgraded subclass advancement in this tier and every other multiclass advancement on your sheet. You can never gain a specialization or mastery from your second class.

Multiclassing Restrictions

  • Force Adept: Multiclassing into the Force Adept requires the GM's approval and either an attuned kyber crystal or an awakening in the Force that the story has built toward.

  • Mechanic: If you already have a droid companion when you take the Mechanic's foundation, gain two upgrades for your droid instead of a second droid.

  • Guardian and Soldier: These classes have no Spellcast trait, so multiclassing into them doesn't give you one. Their cards are all Abilities.

Chapter 5

Kyberheart Mechanics

Kyberheart Mechanics

Rules found only in Kyberheart that don’t need a chapter of their own: the Force, kyber crystals and lightsabers, how character features apply to vehicles, cross-training, ion damage, the stun setting, languages, slicing, smuggling, and bounty hunting. Droid Companions and Starships and Space Combat have their own chapters.

The Force and Damage Types

  • Only the Force deals magic damage. Force Adept spells and Force weapons deal magic damage. Every other card, weapon, and feature deals physical damage, even when it's a Spell.

  • Only Force Adepts wield the Force. In the Daggerheart SRD, magic weapons require a Spellcast trait. In Kyberheart, Force weapons are restricted to Force Adepts, or to a character who has attuned a kyber crystal (see Kyber Crystals and Lightsabers).

  • Spells outside the Force: For every class except the Force Adept, a Spell is a trained technique, like a well-placed bolas throw or a slicing routine, that uses the Spellcast trait.

  • Lightsabers: Every Force weapon counts as a lightsaber for any feature that mentions one.

Kyber Crystals and Lightsabers

Kyber crystals are living crystals attuned to the Force. Every lightsaber is powered by one, and enormous crystals power the Empire's superweapons. Jedi younglings once traveled to the caves of Ilum in a rite called the Gathering to find the crystal that called to them. Others found theirs in temple ruins, on the holy moon of Jedha, or in the hilt of a fallen Jedi.

Starting lightsabers. A Force Adept who starts with a Force weapon already has an attuned crystal inside it. These rules cover finding new crystals, replacing a lost lightsaber, bleeding and healing crystals, and characters of other classes.

Finding a Crystal

Kyber can't be bought on any legal market. A character finds a crystal through the story: answering its call in a sacred cave, recovering one from a ruin or a fallen Jedi, or buying one on the black market for 1 chest of credits from a seller who is probably being watched. Finding a crystal that calls to you makes a fitting goal for a session or a whole arc.

Attuning a Crystal

Attuning a crystal uses the Work on a Project downtime move. Start a progress countdown: 3 for a Force Adept, or 6 for any other character. Each time the character works on the project, they make an Instinct Roll (13); a Force Adept can use their Spellcast trait instead.

ResultProgress
Success with HopeTick down 2
Success with FearTick down 1
FailureNo progress, and the character marks a Stress as the crystal resists

When the countdown ends, the crystal is attuned to that character.

Attuning without being a Force Adept. A character of another class can attune a crystal only if the GM agrees the story supports it, such as a latent sensitivity to the Force, a bond with a Jedi mentor, or a crystal that chose them. Once attuned, they can wield Force weapons. They don't gain Spells or other Force features; for those, they must multiclass into the Force Adept.

Building a Lightsaber

With an attuned crystal, a Tool Kit, and a long rest, a character can build a lightsaber. Choose any Force weapon of your tier or lower from the Equipment chapter, except the Darksaber, and describe its hilt; every lightsaber is personal. Design it in the Lightsaber Workbench. To change its form later, such as converting a single blade into a double-bladed saber, rebuild it during another long rest.

Crystal Colors

A crystal reveals its color when it's attuned. Choose one, or roll a d6: 1–2 blue, 3–4 green, 5 yellow (the color of the Jedi Temple Guards), or 6 purple. Red and white crystals come only from bleeding and healing.

Bleeding a Crystal

A dark side user can force a crystal to obey by pouring their hatred into it until it bleeds red. Bleeding uses Work on a Project with a countdown of 3 and no roll. Each time the character works on it, they mark 2 Stress. In The Dark Times campaign frame, they gain a Darkness token instead.

Healing a Bled Crystal

A bled crystal can be healed, as Ahsoka Tano healed the crystals she took from an Inquisitor. A healed crystal glows white. Healing uses Work on a Project with a countdown of 4 and an Instinct Roll (15), using the progress table above. A character with Darkness tokens can't make progress. When the countdown ends, the character gains 2 Hope.

Losing a Crystal

A lost crystal can be recovered; a destroyed one is gone for good. A crystal stays attuned to its owner, so anyone else who takes it must attune it themselves. Dark side users usually bleed a captured crystal instead.

Characters and Vehicles

When a card, class feature, or item refers to a vehicle's Hit Points, Armor Slots, or Stress, use a starship's Hull, Shield Slots, and Stress. See the Starships and Space Combat chapter.

Cross-Training

For a hint of a second class from level 1, you can trade one of your two starting level 1 class cards for a level 1 card from another class's deck.

  • You don't gain that class's features, subclass, or Spellcast trait. A cross-trained Spell uses your own subclass's Spellcast trait.

  • You can't take Force Adept cards unless the GM grants you an attuned kyber crystal.

  • The cross-trained card stays yours. If you multiclass into that class at level 5, the card counts as one of its cards.

  • Cross-Training and Droid Pal both use one of your starting card choices, so you can't use both.

Example: A player wants a Jedi with a scoundrel's streak. They choose the Force Adept with the Jedi subclass, take Mind Trick, and trade their second card for the Scoundrel's Fast Talker. At level 5, they can multiclass into the Scoundrel for real.

Ion Damage

Ion weapons flood electronics with energy. They hurt living targets like any other blast, but they can shut down a droid, a speeder, or a starship. An ion attack is any attack from a weapon with the Ion feature (such as the Ion Blaster Pistol or a ship's Ion Cannons), an Ion Grenade, or a card that fires an ion charge, such as the Technician's Ion Burst.

TargetWhat an ion attack does
Living creatureTakes the attack's damage as normal.
Droid adversaryTakes the damage and must also mark a Stress.
Droid PCTakes the damage and must also mark a Stress, plus the additional Stress from the Droid ancestry's weakness to ion weapons.
Droid companionMarks a Stress for taking damage, as usual, plus 1 more.
Vehicle or starshipA vehicle takes the damage and must also mark a Stress. A starship hit by ship-scale ion weapons marks Stress instead of Hull, as the Ion feature in the Starships and Space Combat chapter says.

Ionized

When a droid, vehicle, or starship marks its last Stress from an ion attack, its systems lock up: it's temporarily Ionized. While Ionized, it can't use reactions and can't take any other actions until it clears this condition. An Ionized ship drifts; it can't maneuver, fire, or jump to hyperspace. As with any character who marks their last Stress, it's also Vulnerable until it clears at least 1 Stress.

  • Clearing it (PCs): A Droid PC clears Ionized with a successful action roll, usually Knowledge to reboot or Strength to force a restart. On a ship, the Engineer clears it with a Repair Systems roll. Allies can Help as usual.

  • Clearing it (adversaries): As with any temporary condition, the GM puts the spotlight on the adversary and describes how it reboots. This doesn't require a roll, but it uses up that adversary's spotlight.

  • Droid companions: A droid companion that marks its last Stress goes Offline instead, as usual.

  • Other sources: The GM can use these rules for EMP blasts, ion storms, and electrified hazards.

Stun Setting

Most blaster pistols, hold-out blasters, carbines, and rifles have a stun setting, from the stormtroopers who captured Leia aboard the Tantive IV to bounty hunters who need their quarry breathing. Heavy and rotary blasters, sniper rifles, disruptors, bowcasters, ion weapons, and improvised blasters don't.

RuleDetails
Setting your blasterSay you're set for stun before you make an attack. Switching settings is free.
RangeStun bolts lose their punch quickly: a stun attack can only target a creature within Close range.
DamageOn a success, roll damage as normal, then halve it (round down) before comparing it to the target's thresholds. Armor reduces it as usual. The target marks Stress instead of Hit Points: 1 for Minor, 2 for Major, or 3 for Severe damage.
Knocked outWhen a target must mark Stress from a stun attack but can't, it doesn't mark a Hit Point instead. It's knocked out (see below). Minions are knocked out by any stun damage, as their Minion feature says.
ImmuneDroids, vehicles, and creatures the GM rules too big or too strange to stun, like a rancor, shake it off and take no damage.
AdversariesThe GM can declare that any adversary's blaster attack is set for stun, as when the Empire wants prisoners.

Knocked Out

A knocked-out adversary is defeated, which the SRD already allows to mean incapacitated rather than killed. It stays down until the scene ends or someone wakes it.

A knocked-out PC drops unconscious but doesn't make a death move. They can't move or act and don't know what's happening around them. They wake at the end of the scene, or sooner if an ally within Melee range succeeds on an action roll (10) to revive them, usually with Instinct or Knowledge. Because all their Stress is marked, they wake Vulnerable until they clear at least 1 Stress. Waking up in a cell is a classic way to start the next scene.

Bounty Hunters: The Bounty Hunter's Set for Stun card is the specialist's version. It skips the damage roll, marks a Stress, and Restrains the target, with no range limit beyond the blaster's own.

Languages

The Daggerheart SRD doesn't track languages. Kyberheart adds a light rule, because the galaxy is full of them: Chewbacca answers Han in Shyriiwook, Greedo threatens him in Huttese, and R2-D2 only ever beeps.

  • Everyone speaks Galactic Basic and reads Aurebesh.

  • Your ancestry gives you its language, if it has one (see the table below).

  • One more language of your choice. Your community is a good place to look: Mando'a in a Mandalorian Covert, Huttese in a Syndicate, or Bocce for a Spacer.

  • Droid PCs speak Binary as well as Basic. A Droid with an astromech chassis can choose to speak only Binary, like R2-D2; it still understands Basic.

  • Understand, but not speak: Some languages are nearly impossible for other species to speak. Organics can learn to understand Binary but can't speak it, and few non-Wookiees can speak Shyriiwook. Wookiees understand Basic, but their throats can't form it. A Wookiee's crewmates learn to understand Shyriiwook after a session or two together, as Han did.

No Shared Language

When you talk with someone who shares no language with you, you can get across simple ideas with gestures, tone, and pointing. Rolls that depend on being understood have disadvantage, and complex ideas don't get across at all.

An ally who speaks both languages, a protocol droid (such as a droid companion with the Protocol frame), or a translator can bridge the gap and remove the disadvantage. They can also Help an Ally on the roll.

Learning a language: Use Work on a Project as a simple project with a countdown of 6. A teacher, a language program, or a patient protocol droid lowers it by 1.

Galactic Languages

LanguageSpoken by
Galactic BasicAlmost everyone. Its written alphabet is Aurebesh.
BinaryAstromechs and many other droids. Also called Droidspeak.
BocceSpacers and merchants; a common trade language.
HutteseHutts and much of the Outer Rim underworld.
Mando'aMandalorians. Clone troopers use some of its words, too.
ShyriiwookWookiees.
Twi'lekiTwi'leks. It combines spoken words with signs made by the lekku.
RodeseRodians.
DoshTrandoshans.
TogrutiTogruta.
DureseDuros.
SullusteseSullustans.
Mon CalamariMon Calamari.
CheunhChiss, who rarely teach it to outsiders.
Gungan BasicGungans. Anyone who speaks Basic can mostly follow it.
JawaeseJawas.
EwokeseEwoks.

Humans, Zabraks, and Mirialans speak Basic plus one more language of their choice.

Slicing

Slicing is breaking into computers, security systems, and droids. Anyone can try, though Technicians with the Slicer subclass and astromech droids do it best. A slicing roll is an action roll, usually Knowledge, or Finesse for hands-on bypasses like crossing wires in a door panel. A card or feature that slices, such as the Slicer's Kit, uses the roll it describes.

SecurityExamplesDifficultyAccessTrace
CivilianA cantina door, a personal datapad, a moisture farm's droids1036
CommercialA spaceport terminal, a corporate vault, a Hutt's palace1345
ImperialA garrison network, a Star Destroyer's blast doors, a checkpoint scanner1654
Top secretAn ISB archive, the Citadel Tower's data vault on Scarif1963

Quick Slices

A quick slice is one action roll against the system's Difficulty: opening a door, pulling a file from an unguarded terminal, or wiping a droid's memory of the last hour. On a success, it works. On a failure, the GM makes a move as usual, such as tripping an alarm, locking the system, or wasting precious time.

Deep Slices

For a bigger job, like taking over a garrison's security net or cracking an encrypted archive, the GM starts linked progress and consequence countdowns, as in a chase: Access (progress) and Trace (consequence), with the starting values from the table above. Each slicing roll advances both, following the SRD's dynamic countdown chart. Other PCs can keep the slicer covered; their rolls don't advance the countdowns unless they help with the slice itself.

When Access reaches 0, you're in. Choose two:

  • Open, lock, or seal doors throughout the facility.

  • Shut down cameras, alarms, turrets, or a shield generator for the scene.

  • Download data: the GM reveals one secret it holds.

  • Plant a false order, record, or security clearance.

  • Take control of one droid or turret for the scene.

  • Erase the crew's records. In The Dark Times, clear 1 Imperial Heat (once per facility).

When Trace reaches 0, the system catches you and locks you out. The GM chooses one or more: alarms sound, security is on its way, a feedback surge forces the slicer to mark 2 Stress, the data wipes itself, or the slice is traced back to the crew (in The Dark Times, the party gains 1 Imperial Heat).

Slicing Tools

ToolEffect
Slicer KitNeeded for a deep slice. Without one, slicing rolls on a deep slice have disadvantage.
Hacking SpikePlug it into a port to gain advantage on one slicing roll. It burns out after one use.
Encryption KeyAccess starts 1 lower on the system the key was made for.
Imperial Code CylinderTreat an Imperial system as Commercial security.
AstromechAn astromech companion's Interface Port gives it a d8 Help die on slicing rolls.
Restraining BoltA droid fitted with one can't act against whoever holds its controller. Removing one is a quick slice (10), or takes a Tool Kit and a moment of calm.

Smuggling

Smuggling pays for a lot of fuel: moving cargo past customs officers, rival gangs, and the occasional Star Destroyer. A smuggling job pays as the Earning Credits table in the Equipment chapter says for its tier, and illegal cargo pays double.

Contraband

LegalityExamplesIf it's found
LegalFood, machine parts, ordinary medical suppliesNothing. It moves freely, though officials may still want their cut.
RestrictedMilitary-grade blasters, unlicensed droids, bacta bound for a war zoneIt's seized unless the crew has a permit.
IllegalSpice, coaxium, kyber, Rebel weapons, stolen Imperial techIt's seized, and the crew faces arrest or a heavy fine.

Legality depends on who's in charge. Rebel weapons are illegal anywhere the Empire rules, and a Hutt doesn't care what the Empire thinks.

Inspections

When the crew faces an inspection, such as customs at a spaceport, an Imperial checkpoint, or a boarding party, the GM calls for an action roll from whoever leads the deception. Use the environment's Difficulty if there is one, such as the Spaceport Docking Bay's Papers, Please. Pick an approach: Presence to bluff, Finesse to hide or swap cargo, or Knowledge to present forged manifests. Other crew members can Help an Ally, or the GM can call for a Group Action Roll.

  • Advantage: Cargo hidden in Smuggling Compartments, or people carrying Forged Imperial IDs.

  • Bribes: Before rolling, you can offer a bribe of 1 to 3 handfuls of credits to gain advantage on the roll. On a failure, the inspector keeps the bribe anyway.

  • On a failure, the GM chooses one or more: the contraband is seized, the crew pays a fine, the inspectors plant a tracker, the party gains 1 Imperial Heat (in The Dark Times), or the officers move to arrest the crew, which leads to a fight or a chase.

Dumping Cargo

At any moment before an inspection or during a chase, the crew can jettison its cargo, as Han Solo did. An inspection finds nothing, and in a chase the Escape countdown ticks down 1. But the cargo is gone, and the crew now owes the client a debt equal to twice the job's payout.

Debts

A debt is credits owed to a crime lord, a syndicate, or an angry client. Note the amount and the creditor on the ship's log or your character sheet.

  • Interest: While a debt is unpaid, once per session the GM can bring it into the story as a complication: an enforcer collecting, a "favor" that can't be refused, or a rival who bought the debt. When they do, each PC who owes it gains a Hope.

  • Deadline: If the debt isn't paid by the deadline the creditor set, a bounty goes out on everyone who owes it.

  • Paying up: Pay the credits, then settle it with the "Pay off a debt to a crime lord" project in Projects During Downtime.

Bounty Hunting

Bounties come from a guild, a crime lord, or the Empire, usually on a bounty puck: a small holoprojector showing the target, the terms, and the reward. The reward uses the Earning Credits table for the target's tier.

TermsReward
AliveThe full reward. The Stun Setting and a set of Restraints help.
Dead or aliveThe full reward for a live target, or half for a dead one.
DeadThe full reward, with proof.

  • Tracking: Finding a target who has gone to ground is a progress countdown: 4 for a careless target, or 6 for a professional. Advance it with Instinct or Presence rolls, such as following tracks or asking around a cantina. A Tracking Fob keyed to the target lowers it by 1.

  • The Guild code: Guild hunters don't interfere with another member's active bounty. A hunter who breaks the code loses their guild standing, and the guild may post a bounty on them.

Sabacc

Sabacc is played in cantinas, casinos, and cargo holds across the galaxy. The Sabacc tool has the full rules for Corellian Spike, Coruscant Shift, and Kessel Sabacc.

Roll It or Play It

  • When the game is scenery, resolve it with one roll, such as the Wretched Hive Cantina’s High-Stakes Sabacc feature: a Presence or Instinct Roll.

  • When the story turns on the hand, such as winning a ship, a debt, a map, or a secret, deal a real hand at the table using any version from the Sabacc tool.

Stakes

  • Chips are credits: One chip is worth a handful of credits (see Counting Credits). At richer tables, each chip is worth a bag. The credit chip tokens in Downloads work as betting chips.

  • Other stakes: Ships, debts, favors, and secrets can go in the pot. The GM decides what each is worth before the deal.

  • NPC players: The GM plays each NPC’s hand and can bluff. A Sabacc Shark makes a good rival.

Playing Your Character

These are action rolls, so a relevant Experience (such as Sabacc Shark or Gambler) can add to them as usual.

  • Read the table: Before the reveal, make an Instinct Roll against an opponent’s Difficulty. On a success, the GM tells you whether they’re bluffing.

  • Talk them out of it: Make a Presence Roll to pressure one NPC into junking their hand before the reveal. On a failure, they call, and they remember it.

  • Cheat: Make a Finesse Roll to swap one card in your hand for a card you hid earlier. On a success, nobody notices. On a failure, someone does, and the GM chooses the consequence: a brawl, a bounty, a ban, or more Heat.

Shift Tokens as Loot

Kessel Sabacc shift tokens make good small rewards. They turn up on a gambler’s body, in a smuggler’s stash, or as a cantina tournament prize. Players keep their tokens and choose three to bring to each game.

Equipment

Equipment

Equipment Rules

RuleDetails
Active gearOne Primary weapon, one Secondary weapon, and one armor. You can also carry two inventory weapons. You can't equip gear with a higher tier than yours.
Swapping weaponsSwap an inventory weapon with an active weapon of the same burden for free during a rest or moment of calm; otherwise, mark a Stress to do so.
BurdenMaximum burden is 2 hands. A Two-Handed Primary leaves no hand for a Secondary.
DamageRoll a number of damage dice equal to your Proficiency. A flat modifier (the "+3" in d8+3) is added once and isn't multiplied by Proficiency.
Tier progressionPrimary weapons gain +3 flat damage per tier. Secondary weapons gain +2 per tier, and their Paired, Protective, and Barrier values rise by 1 per tier. Armor thresholds are listed in the Armor tables.
Force weaponsForce weapons are restricted to Force Adepts or a character who has attuned a kyber crystal.
LightsabersEvery Force weapon counts as a lightsaber for any feature that mentions one, such as the Jedi's Lightsaber Defense, Beskar, and Cortosis.
UnarmoredUse the SRD's unarmored rules: your base Armor Score is 0.
Stun settingMost blasters can be set for stun. See Stun Setting.
ThrowingYou can throw an equipped weapon at a target within Very Close range with a Finesse roll. It's no longer equipped until you retrieve it.

Weapon Features

FeatureEffect
Barrier+X to Armor Score; −1 to Evasion.
BrutalWhen you roll the maximum value on a damage die, roll an additional damage die.
Cumbersome−1 to Finesse.
Flexible+1 to Evasion.
Heavy−1 to Evasion.
HookedOn a successful attack, you can pull the target into Melee range.
Paired+X to primary weapon damage to targets within Melee range.
PowerfulOn a successful attack, roll an additional damage die and discard the lowest result.
Protective+X to Armor Score.
QuickWhen you make an attack, you can mark a Stress to target another creature within range.
Reliable+1 to attack rolls.
Beskar (weapon)This weapon can block a lightsaber. When a lightsaber attack targets you, you can spend a Hope to gain a +2 bonus to your Evasion against it.
ConcealedYou have advantage on rolls to hide this weapon, and a casual search won't find it.
IonOn a successful attack against a droid or vehicle, the target must mark a Stress. See Ion Damage.
ParryWhen a ranged attack targets you, you can spend a Hope to gain a +2 bonus to your Evasion against it.
SpinningWhen you make an attack, you can mark a Stress to target another creature within Melee range.
SplashOn a successful attack, you can mark a Stress to deal half the damage to each other adversary within Very Close range of the target.
StunningWhen you succeed with Hope on an attack, the target has disadvantage on its next attack roll.
Symbol of MandaloreOnce per rest, when you succeed on an attack with this weapon, gain a Hope. Mandalorians recognize it on sight.

Credit Economy

Daggerheart tracks wealth in handfuls, bags, and chests of gold. Kyberheart keeps the same structure as credits.

DenominationValueDescription
Handful1 handfulLoose credit chips: enough for a meal, a night's lodging, or a basic item.
Bag10 handfulsA credit pouch or a stack of data-chits.
Chest10 bagsA credit case or bank draft.

  • Rolling over: As in the SRD, when you'd gain a handful while holding 9, mark a bag and clear your handfuls instead; bags roll into a chest the same way.

  • Holding limit: You can't hold more than 1 chest. Spend credits or store them somewhere, such as a ship, safehouse, or bank, before you can gain more.

  • Starting wealth: Each character starts with 1 handful of credits.

  • Currency: Galactic credits are the common standard (Republic, Imperial, or New Republic depending on the era). Outer Rim worlds also deal in Hutt currencies such as wupiupi, peggats, and truguts, which many refuse to swap for Republic credits.

Counting Credits

Credits stay abstract, like gold in the SRD. When an NPC names a price in credits, use this conversion:

DenominationAboutFor scale
Handful100 creditsA meal and a bunk at a spaceport.
Bag1,000 creditsObi-Wan paid Han Solo 2,000 credits up front: 2 bags.
Chest10,000 creditsHan's asking price to fly two passengers and two droids to Alderaan.

Credit chips (optional): For finer tracking, use the SRD's optional coins rule: 10 credit chips equal 1 handful, so each chip is worth about 10 credits. Physical credit chips at the table work well for this.

Buying and Selling

  • Haggling: Before you buy or sell, you can make a Presence Roll against the merchant's Difficulty: 10 for a friendly trader, 13 for most dealers, or 16 for a tough one, like a Toydarian junk dealer who can't be fooled by a Jedi mind trick. On a success, lower the price by 1 handful (or by 1 bag for items priced in bags, but never below 1 handful), or sell an item for its full price instead of half. On a failure with Fear, the merchant won't deal with you again today.

  • Black market: Restricted and illegal goods (see Contraband in Kyberheart Mechanics) are sold only through fences and syndicates, at double the listed price. A fence buys them back at the full listed price.

  • Smuggling and bounties: Smuggling runs and bounties pay by the Earning Credits table. See Smuggling and Bounty Hunting in Kyberheart Mechanics.
