Chapter 7

Droid Companions

Droid Companions

Rules at a Glance

A droid companion is a loyal droid that travels with your character. It uses the SRD's Ranger Companion rules with a Star Wars frame on top. It isn't a second character: it acts when you command it.

RuleDetails
SheetEvasion, Stress slots, two Experiences at +2, a Standard Attack, a Frame Feature, and upgrades.
CommandMake a Spellcast Roll to command your droid to take an action. You can spend a Hope to add one of its Experiences to the roll. On a success with Hope, if your next action builds on its success, you gain advantage on that roll.
No Spellcast trait?Guardians and Soldiers choose Instinct or Knowledge as their command trait when they gain a droid.
AttackWhen you command your droid to attack, it gains any benefits that would normally apply only to you. On a success, its damage roll uses your Proficiency and its damage die.
Help an AllyYou can spend a Hope to have your droid Help an Ally instead of you. It rolls a d6 advantage die, or a d8 when its Frame Feature applies.
Taking damageAttacks against your droid use its Evasion. When it would take any amount of damage, it marks a Stress.
OfflineWhen your droid marks its last Stress, it goes Offline and drops out of the scene. It returns at the start of your next long rest with 1 Stress cleared, or sooner with the Repair Droid downtime move.
RecoveringWhen you choose a downtime move that clears Stress on yourself, your droid clears an equal number of Stress.
Independent actionOnce per rest, your droid can take one action on its own, without a command roll, as long as it fits its programming.
Gaining ExperiencesWhenever you gain a new Experience, your droid also gains one at +2.

Getting a Droid

Way to get oneWhat you get
Mechanic (Technician subclass)A full droid companion as the Mechanic's foundation feature. Choose an upgrade every time you level up, as a Beastbound Ranger does for their companion.
Droid Pal (any class)At character creation, trade one of your two starting level 1 class cards for a droid companion. It starts with one upgrade and gains another each time you gain a new Experience (levels 2, 5, and 8).

A Droid ancestry PC is already a droid, but can still keep a droid companion.

Building Your Droid

  1. Frame: Pick a frame from the table below. It sets your droid's Evasion, Stress slots, and Frame Feature.

  2. Name and look: Give your droid a name, a color scheme, and any markings.

  3. Experiences: Create two Experiences at +2 based on its frame and history.

  4. Standard Attack: Pick one from the Standard Attacks table.

  5. Starting upgrade (Droid Pal only): Pick one upgrade. A Mechanic's droid gains its first upgrade at level 2.

  6. Quirk: Roll or choose a quirk.

  7. Reprogrammed (optional): Apply the Reprogrammed modifier.

Droid Frames

Astromech

Evasion 10 · Stress 3

Like R2-D2, BB-8, Chopper, R5-D4.

Interface Port: Its Help die is a d8 on slicing, repair, and piloting rolls.

Suggested Experiences: Slicing, Starfighter Repair, Astrogation

Protocol

Evasion 10 · Stress 3

Like C-3PO, TC-14.

Translator: It understands and speaks almost any language. Its Help die is a d8 on negotiating, etiquette, and translating rolls.

Suggested Experiences: Etiquette, Languages, Customs and Protocol

Combat

Evasion 10 · Stress 3

Like B1 and B2 battle droids, BX commando droids.

Programmed for War: Its Help die is a d8 on attack rolls.

Suggested Experiences: Tactics, Weapons Handling, Squad Drills

Heavy

Evasion 9 · Stress 4

Like K-2SO, IG-11, IG-88.

Imposing Frame: Its Help die is a d8 on intimidating and protecting.

Suggested Experiences: Security Protocols, Intimidation, Hand-to-Hand

Scout

Evasion 11 · Stress 2

Like BD-1, MSE-6 mouse droids, probe droids.

Tiny Frame: It fits through tight spaces. Its Help die is a d8 on perceiving and navigating.

Suggested Experiences: Scanning, Stealth, Climbing

Medical

Evasion 10 · Stress 3

Like 2-1B, FX-7.

Medical Protocols: Once per rest, it can clear a Hit Point on an ally within Very Close range.

Suggested Experiences: Field Medicine, Bacta Care, Triage

Labor

Evasion 9 · Stress 4

Like GNK power droids, pit droids, Treadwell droids.

Heavy Lifter: Its Help die is a d8 on Strength Rolls, and it can carry one large item or an unconscious ally.

Suggested Experiences: Repair, Hauling, Maintenance

Eccentric

Evasion 10 · Stress 3

Like D-O, L3-37, L0-LA59 ("Lola").

Scene Stealer: Once per rest, when its personality changes a scene by charming, distracting, or inspiring someone, you or an ally gains a Hope.

Suggested Experiences: Charm, Showmanship, Street Smarts

Reprogrammed (optional modifier)

Apply this to any frame to make a repurposed security, battle, or assassin droid, like K-2SO or IG-11. Your droid gains:

  • Former Function: An additional Experience at +2 that reflects its original programming.

  • Residual Directive: Once per session, the GM can invoke a directive from its old programming as a complication. When they do, you gain a Hope.

Standard Attacks

At level 1, a droid's attack uses either a d6 at Melee range or a d4 at Close range. The Vicious Weapons upgrade improves the die or the range by one step.

AttackRangeDamage
Shock ProdMeleed6 phy
Tool Arm or Welding TorchMeleed6 phy
Heavy Fists (Heavy and Labor frames)Meleed6 phy
Hold-Out BlasterClosed4 phy
Blaster Arm (Combat and Heavy frames)Closed4 phy
Distraction ZapperClosed4 phy

Upgrades

An upgrade can be taken once unless its Max says otherwise, and only at or above its Tier.

Tier 1+ Level 1 and up

Resilient Core

Tier 1+ · Take up to 3 times

Your droid gains an additional Stress slot.

Evasive Servos

Tier 1+ · Take once

Your droid gains a permanent +2 bonus to its Evasion.

Vicious Weapons

Tier 1+ · Take up to 3 times

Increase your droid's damage die or range by one step (d6 to d8, Melee to Close, and so on).

Armored Chassis

Tier 1+ · Take once

When your droid takes damage, you can mark one of your Armor Slots instead of one of its Stress.

Upgraded Programming

Tier 1+ · Take up to 3 times

Your droid gains a permanent +1 bonus to an Experience of your choice.

Trusted Partner

Tier 1+ · Take once

Use this as an additional Hope slot your character can mark.

Maintenance Time

Tier 1+ · Take once

Once per rest, when you take time during a quiet moment to tune up your droid, you can gain a Hope, or you and your droid can both clear a Stress.

Emergency Protocol

Tier 1+ · Take once

When you mark your last Hit Point, your droid rushes to your side. Roll a number of d6s equal to its unmarked Stress slots and mark them. If any roll a 6, your droid gets you back up: clear your last Hit Point and return to the scene.

Sensor Suite

Tier 1+ · Take once

Once per rest, when your droid scans an area, ask the GM one question about it. The GM answers honestly.

Tool Mount

Tier 1+ · Take once

Once per rest, when you repair, slice, or modify something with your droid within Very Close range, roll with advantage.

Utility Compartment

Tier 1+ · Take once

Once per session, spend a Hope to have your droid produce a mundane item from its compartment that's useful to your situation.

Medical Module

Tier 1+ · Take once

Once per rest, when you use the Tend to Wounds downtime move with your droid's help, clear 1 additional Hit Point.

Tier 2+ Level 2 and up

Thrusters

Tier 2+ · Take once

Your droid can fly. Once per rest, it can carry one ally within Close range along with it.

Shield Projector

Tier 2+ · Take once

Your droid can mark a Stress to give an ally within Close range a +2 bonus to their Evasion against one attack.

Guardian Protocol

Tier 2+ · Take once

Once per rest, when an attack targets an ally within Very Close range of your droid, it can mark a Stress to become the target instead.

Intimidation Subroutine

Tier 2+ · Take once

When your droid succeeds on an attack, the target must mark a Stress.

Tier 3+ Level 5 and up

Loyalty Protocol

Tier 3+ · Take once

Once per long rest, when the damage from an attack would mark your droid's last Stress or your last Hit Point and you're within Close range of each other, you or your droid can rush to the other's side and take that damage instead.

Droids in Play

SituationHow it works
CombatCommand your droid to attack, move, or act. It acts as part of your spotlight, not on its own turn.
ExplorationAdd its Experiences to command rolls when it scans, slices, carries, or scouts. Its Frame Feature boosts its Help die in its specialty.
SocialProtocol and Eccentric frames shine here, and quirks can complicate or help a scene.
DowntimeYour droid clears Stress when you do (see Recovering) and can be repaired with the Repair Droid downtime move.
Capture or theftThe GM can capture, steal, or reprogram a droid as a story complication.

Repair Droid (downtime move)

During a short or long rest, with a Tool Kit, you can choose this downtime move instead of another: clear 1d4 Stress on a droid. If the droid was Offline, it comes back online.

The Technician's Field Medic and Patch Job cards also work on droids.

Quirks

Roll a d10 or choose. Once per session, when your droid's quirk causes trouble for you or the party, you gain a Hope.

d10QuirkInspired by
1Worrier: Constantly quotes odds and frets about danger.C-3PO
2Blunt Statistician: States probabilities with brutal honesty.K-2SO
3Sassy: Answers in rude beeps and whistles.R2-D2
4Cantankerous: Grumbles and schemes, but would never abandon its crew.Chopper
5Overprotective: Fusses over your safety.Nursemaid droids, Lola

Chapter 8

Starships and Space Combat

Starships and Space Combat

This chapter covers everything in space, in five parts: how space combat works (the sheet, stations, maneuvers, crew actions, and weapons), keeping the ship flying (damage, systems, repairs, and death moves), your crew's ship (getting one, the ship catalog, upgrades, and refits), situations (chases, hyperspace, and boarding), and running space combat for the GM. Speeders, swoops, and walkers have their own chapter: Ground Vehicles.

Space Combat at a Glance

Space combat uses the same rules as every other Daggerheart scene: the spotlight, Duality Dice, ranges, Hope and Fear, Stress, damage thresholds, and countdowns. A PC ship has a sheet like a companion's; an enemy ship is an adversary stat block. Crew members take the spotlight at their stations and make action rolls as usual.

RuleDetails
ShipsA PC ship has a Starship Sheet: Evasion, Hull, Stress, Shield Slots, damage thresholds, Speed, and weapons. Enemy ships use adversary stat blocks.
SpotlightThere's no initiative. Crew members act from their stations when the spotlight is on them, following the SRD's normal spotlight rules.
RangeMelee is docked or colliding; Very Close is a tight dogfight; Close is typical weapons range; Far is long-range fire; Very Far is sensor range.
AttacksPCs roll against the target's Difficulty. Enemy ships roll against your ship's Evasion.
DamageCompare damage to the ship's thresholds and mark Hull: 1 for Minor, 2 for Major, 3 for Severe damage, and, if you use the SRD's optional massive damage rule, 4 when damage is double the Severe threshold or more.
ShieldsMark a Shield Slot to reduce the severity of incoming damage by one threshold.
StressShip Stress is system strain, marked when you push the ship. When the ship must mark Stress but has none left, it marks a Hull instead. When it marks its last Stress, a Critical System fails.
ConditionsShips use the standard conditions: Hidden (in cover or off sensors), Restrained (tractor beam or docking clamp), and Vulnerable (locked on, so all rolls targeting it have advantage).
CountdownsChases, jumps, and set pieces use the SRD's progress and consequence countdowns.

Ships and Character Features

When a card, class feature, or item refers to a vehicle's Hit Points, Armor Slots, or Stress, use the ship's Hull, Shield Slots, and Stress. For example, the Technician's I Can Fix This clears Hull or Shield Slots, and the Pilot's Brace for Impact marks an extra Shield Slot.

A Round in Space

Here's how a fight flows. The crew's YT-1300 is jumped by two TIE fighters as it leaves Ord Mantell.

  1. The GM sets the scene. The TIEs dive in at Close range and attack, rolling against the freighter's Evasion (10). One hits for 9 damage: Major against its thresholds (8 / 16), so 2 Hull. The pilot marks a Shield Slot to drop it to Minor, and the ship marks 1 Hull.
  2. The pilot makes a maneuver. Get on Its Tail is an Agility Roll against the TIE's Difficulty. On a success, the lead TIE is Vulnerable, so every roll against it has advantage.
  3. The gunner fires. They roll with the quad laser turret's trait against the TIE's Difficulty, with advantage. On a hit, they roll damage dice equal to their own Proficiency.
  4. The engineer pushes the ship. Overload marks a ship Stress to give the pilot advantage on their next roll.
  5. The GM answers. When a roll fails or comes up with Fear, the GM makes a move: another TIE swoops in, or the shields flicker.

Scale

ScaleExamples
0: PersonalCharacters, droids, speeder bikes
1: FighterX-wing, TIE fighter
2: FreighterYT-1300, Lambda-class shuttle
3: CapitalCR90 corvette, Star Destroyer

When the attacker's scale is smaller than the target's, reduce the severity of the damage by one threshold for each step of difference; damage reduced below Minor has no effect. When the attacker is larger, increase the severity by one threshold for each step. Personal weapons can't normally harm ships, but a character can still sabotage, board, or slice into one.

Some weapons and features break the scale rule on purpose, such as a Bomber's torpedoes against capital ships.

Fighters against a Star Destroyer? See Running Capital Ship Battles.

The Starship Sheet

FieldMeaning
Name, Scale, TierWhat the ship is and which tier of play it suits.
EvasionThe number enemy attack rolls must meet or beat.
HullThe ship's Hit Points, marked by damage severity.
StressSystem strain, marked when you push the ship.
Shield SlotsMark one to reduce the severity of incoming damage by one threshold.
Damage ThresholdsMajor and Severe. Unlike a character's, they don't add your level.
SpeedSlow, Standard, Fast, or Blazing (sublight chases and maneuvers).
Hyperdrive ClassHow fast the ship travels through hyperspace.
WeaponsTrait, range, and damage. Ship weapons roll damage dice equal to the gunner's Proficiency.
StationsThe crew positions aboard.
Features and UpgradesThe ship's special abilities and modifications.

Speed

SpeedEffect
SlowDisadvantage on rolls to escape or catch a faster ship.
StandardNo modifier.
FastAdvantage on rolls to escape or catch a slower ship.
BlazingAs Fast, and when you move, you can move one additional range.

Hyperdrive Class

A lower class is faster. Hyperdrive class affects travel time, not sublight Speed: the Millennium Falcon has a Class 0.5 hyperdrive, while most starfighters and Star Destroyers use Class 1 or 2.

ClassTravel time
0.5One step faster than the route's listed time (a long rest becomes a short rest).
1The route's listed time.
2The listed time, but pursuers with a faster hyperdrive arrive first.
3 or higherOne step slower than the listed time.

Stations and Crew

A character at a station uses that station's trait for its actions, and can man only one station at a time. A starfighter has one or two stations; a light freighter usually has four or five. A character with no station can still act normally, such as repairing a panel, helping, or repelling boarders.

StationTraitStation actions
PilotAgilityManeuvers
GunnerThe weapon's traitFire, Focus Fire, Point Defense
NavigatorKnowledge or InstinctPlot a Course, Scan, Call Out Threats
EngineerKnowledgeRepair Systems, Reroute Power, Overload
CommsPresenceHail, Jam Signals, Coordinate

Droids aboard: A droid companion can't man a station, but its owner can command it as usual or spend a Hope to have it Help an Ally. An Astromech's Interface Port gives it a d8 Help die on piloting and repair rolls, and an Astromech Socket lets it ride along in a starfighter.

All hands: When the whole crew works on one task, such as an emergency jump, use the SRD's Group Action Roll. One character leads with an action roll; each other crew member makes a reaction roll, adding +1 to the leader's roll for each success and −1 for each failure.

Roll Results in Space

Action rolls in space follow the SRD's standard outcomes.

ResultWhat happens
Critical SuccessYou succeed with a bonus, gain a Hope, and clear a Stress, either yours or the ship's.
Success with HopeYou succeed and gain a Hope.
Success with FearYou succeed with a cost or complication, and the GM gains a Fear. For example, the ship marks a Stress or an enemy moves into position.
Failure with HopeYou fail with a minor consequence and gain a Hope, then the spotlight swings to the GM.
Failure with FearYou fail with a major consequence and the GM gains a Fear, then the spotlight swings to the GM.

Pilot Maneuvers

Unless noted, roll Agility against the opposing ship's Difficulty, or against the tier's Difficulty for hazards (Tier 1: 11, Tier 2: 14, Tier 3: 17, Tier 4: 20).

Evasive Action

Pilot station

On a success, your ship gains a +2 bonus to its Evasion until an attack succeeds against it or the scene ends.

Get on Its Tail

Pilot station

On a success, move within Very Close range of a target. It becomes temporarily Vulnerable as you lock on.

Shake the Tail

Pilot station

On a success, clear a lock or the Vulnerable condition from your ship and move up to one range away.

Afterburn

Pilot station

Mark a ship Stress to move anywhere within Far range without a roll.

Strafing Run

Pilot station

Mark a ship Stress and make an attack against up to two targets within Very Close range of each other. Roll damage once and apply it to each target you hit.

Ram

Pilot station

On a success, roll d10s equal to your Proficiency and add 4, plus 3 for each tier above 1, for damage, adjusted for scale. Your ship marks 1 Hull. On a failure, your ship marks 2 Hull.

Slip Through

Pilot station

On a success against a hazard, you pass it without harm. Each pursuer must succeed on a Reaction Roll (Agility) with a Difficulty equal to your roll's result, or mark a Stress.

Draw Fire

Pilot station

Spend a Hope. Enemy attacks that would target an allied ship within Close range target your ship instead, until an attack succeeds against your ship or the scene ends.

Dock and Clamp

Pilot station

On a success, move into Melee range and clamp the target. It becomes Restrained, and you can begin boarding.

Pilot Class Features in Space

  • Ace Pilot: Advantage on maneuver rolls.

  • Evasive: Adds its die to the ship's Evasion against an attack.

  • Maneuver: On a success with Hope, the ship can move one additional range.

  • Impossible Maneuver: Automatically succeeds on one maneuver, with no Hope or Fear generated.

  • Pilot cards: Punch It, Lock On, Brace for Impact, Strafing Pass, and Trench Run all work at the controls.

Crew Actions

Gunner

Fire

Gunner station

Roll: Weapon trait vs. Difficulty

Make an attack. On a success, deal the weapon's damage.

Focus Fire

Gunner station

Roll: Group Action Roll or Tag Team Roll

Two or more gunners combine their attacks on one target.

Point Defense

Gunner station

Roll: Reaction Roll (Agility)

When a missile or torpedo targets your ship, spend a Hope and roll against the attack's result. On a success, it's shot down.

Navigator

Plot a Course

Navigator station

Roll: Knowledge or Instinct

Set a hyperspace route (see Hyperspace).

Scan

Navigator station

Roll: Instinct vs. Difficulty

On a success, ask the GM one question about an enemy ship, such as its thresholds, weak points, or next move. On a success with Hope, ask two.

Call Out Threats

Navigator station

Roll: None

Spend a Hope to Help an Ally at the Pilot or Gunner station.

Engineer

Repair Systems

Engineer station

Roll: Knowledge vs. tier Difficulty

On a success, clear a ship Stress, or 2 on a success with Hope. On a failure, the ship marks a Stress.

Reroute Power

Engineer station

Roll: Knowledge vs. tier Difficulty

Mark a ship Stress to clear a Shield Slot, or to restore one Critical System until the end of the scene.

Overload

Engineer station

Roll: None

Mark a ship Stress to give the Pilot or a Gunner advantage on their next roll.

Comms

Hail

Comms station

Roll: Presence

Talk, bluff, or negotiate with another ship.

Jam Signals

Comms station

Roll: Knowledge vs. Difficulty

On a success, one enemy ship has disadvantage on its next attack roll, and it can't call for reinforcements until it clears the jamming.

Coordinate

Comms station

Roll: None

Spend a Hope to Help an Ally with any ship action, rolling a d8 advantage die.

Ship Weapons

Gunners roll with the weapon's trait against the target's Difficulty. Ship weapons roll damage dice equal to the gunner's Proficiency, and add +3 flat damage for each tier above Tier 1, using the ship's tier. Each ship in the Ship Catalog lists its weapons with that bonus already added.

WeaponTraitRangeDamageFeature
Laser CannonsAgilityFard8+2 phy—
Heavy Laser CannonsAgilityFard10+3 phy—
Quad Laser TurretAgilityFard8+2 phyQuick
Rear Laser TurretAgilityClosed8+2 phyCan fire at a ship that has your ship Vulnerable from a lock.
Rotary Blaster CannonAgilityClosed8+3 phy—
Ion CannonsAgilityClosed8 phyIon
Concussion MissilesFinesseFard10+2 phyLimited (2)
Proton TorpedoesFinesseFard10+4 phyLimited (2); Powerful
Ion TorpedoesFinesseFard10+2 phyLimited (2); Ion
Seismic ChargesFinesseClosed10+4 phyLimited (2); Splash
Tractor BeamStrengthClose—On a success, the target is Restrained.
Turbolaser BatteryFinesseVery Fard12+4 phyCapital ships only. Slow Tracking: Attacks against Fighter-scale ships have disadvantage.
Point-Defense LasersAgilityClosed8+2 phyCapital ships only. Screen: Gunners have advantage on Point Defense.

Weapon features:

  • Ion: A hit marks ship Stress instead of Hull, equal to the Hull it would have marked. A ship with no Stress left marks Hull instead, as usual.
  • Limited (X): You can fire this weapon X times. It reloads during a rest.
  • Powerful: On a successful attack, roll an additional damage die and discard the lowest result.
  • Quick: When you make an attack, you can mark a Stress to target another ship within range.
  • Splash: On a successful attack, you can mark a ship Stress to deal half the damage to each other enemy within Very Close range of the target.
  • Capital ships only: Only Capital-scale ships carry this weapon. Slow Tracking gives attacks against Fighter-scale ships disadvantage; Screen gives gunners advantage on Point Defense.

Damage, Systems, and Repairs

Taking Damage

  1. Compare the damage to the ship's thresholds. Below Major is Minor (1 Hull), Major or more is 2 Hull, and Severe or more is 3 Hull.
  2. Adjust for scale. One threshold down for each step the attacker is smaller, one up for each step it's larger (see Scale).
  3. Mark a Shield Slot, if one is free, to reduce the severity by one more threshold.
  4. Mark the Hull. If it's the ship's last Hull, the pilot chooses a ship death move.

Stress runs alongside Hull. The ship marks Stress when it's pushed: maneuvers, overloads, and complications. When it must mark Stress but has none left, it marks a Hull instead, and when it marks its last Stress, a Critical System fails.

Critical Systems

When the ship marks its last Stress, roll a d6 or let the GM choose a Critical System to fail. It stays down until repaired.

d6SystemEffect while down
1EnginesThe ship can't move beyond Very Close range.
2WeaponsThe ship can't attack.
3ShieldsThe ship can't mark Shield Slots.
4SensorsNavigator and Comms actions have disadvantage.
5Life SupportStart a consequence countdown (4). At 0, the crew must evacuate or each marks a Hit Point.
6HyperdriveThe ship can't jump.

Repairs

WhenRepair
In combatAn Engineer's Repair Systems or Reroute Power.
Short restPatch Up (downtime move, needs a Tool Kit): Clear 1d4 + your tier in ship Stress and Shield Slots, in any combination, or fix one Critical System.
Long restOverhaul (downtime move, needs a Tool Kit): Clear all ship Stress and Shield Slots, fix all Critical Systems, and clear 1d4 Hull.
DrydockSpend credits to clear all Hull: 1 handful per Hull at Tier 1, 2 handfuls at Tier 2, 1 bag at Tier 3, and 2 bags at Tier 4.

Ship Death Moves

When a ship marks its last Hull, the pilot chooses one of these.

  • Blaze of Glory: Take one final action with the ship. It automatically critically succeeds. Then the ship is destroyed; the crew escapes in pods or a shuttle if the fiction allows.

  • Crash Landing: Make an Agility Roll against the tier's Difficulty. On a success, the ship survives but is out of the scene until repaired at a drydock. On a failure, the crew survives but the ship is lost.

  • Risk It All: Roll your Duality Dice. If the Hope Die is higher, the ship holds together and clears Hull equal to the Hope Die's value. If the Fear Die is higher, the ship is destroyed. If they match, clear all Hull and Stress.

Your Crew's Ship

Most crews share one ship: a home, a getaway, and a character in its own right. This part covers getting one, the full catalog, and how a ship grows with the crew.

Getting Your First Ship

Choose the crew's ship together at session zero, with the GM. Start with a Tier 1 ship.

Your crewA good fit
A mixed crew (the usual)One Tier 1 freighter, like the YT-1300, the Ghost, the Razor Crest, or the Firespray-31. There's a station for nearly everyone.
A crew of pilotsA Tier 1 fighter for each pilot, flying together as a squadron. Fighters have one or two stations, so anyone else needs a ride.
BothA freighter for the crew, plus a fighter for a pilot who wants their own. The Ghost does this out of the box: its Phantom shuttle detaches as a second ship.

Then answer a few questions about the ship, the way you would for a character. Who owns it on paper? What does the crew still owe on it, and to whom? What always breaks at the worst moment? Where does everyone end up sitting when there's nothing to do? Keep the answers in the ship's notes in the Starship tool.

Ships you don't own. A mission can hand the crew borrowed ships, like Rebel X-wings for a single attack. Use their catalog stats; the ships go back, or don't, when the mission ends.

Ship tier. A ship's tier should match the party's tier. A ship above it is a story reward that comes with trouble: someone wants it back.

Every ship a crew can fly, sorted by tier. At Tier 1, a ship's Evasion and Hull add up to 15 or 16, plus about 1 per tier after that, so a nimble ship trades durability for defense. Filter the list, or add a ship straight to the Starship tool.

Ship Upgrades

Each ship has 2 upgrade slots at Tier 1, plus 1 more per tier. Each upgrade can be installed once per ship. In the Starship tool, installed upgrades fill the ship's slots as cards.

Reinforced Hull

Install once per ship

+1 Hull slot.

Shield Generator

Install once per ship

+1 Shield Slot.

Engine Boost

Install once per ship

+1 to Evasion.

Weapon Upgrade

Install once per ship

Increase one weapon's damage die by one size.

Sensor Array

Install once per ship

Advantage on Scan.

Escape Pods

Install once per ship

The crew always survives the ship's destruction.

Astromech Socket

Install once per ship

A droid companion can ride along and Help.

Hyperdrive Upgrade

Install once per ship

Improve the Hyperdrive Class by one step.

Smuggling Compartments

Install once per ship

Cargo and passengers hidden aboard can't be found by an ordinary search; finding them takes a Finesse or Instinct Roll (16). You have advantage on rolls to hide cargo during inspections.

Refitting and Trading Up

Refitting. At a drydock, a crew can refit their ship to the next tier, so a favorite Tier 1 ship can stay with them all campaign. A refit takes a long rest and costs the same as armor of the new tier (Tier 2: 5 handfuls, Tier 3: 3 bags, Tier 4: 1 chest). The refitted ship:

  • adds +3 to its Major threshold and +6 to its Severe threshold, matching ships built for the new tier;
  • gains 1 Hull or 1 Stress slot;
  • gains 1 upgrade slot;
  • deals the new tier's weapon damage (+3 for each tier above Tier 1).

Trading up. A crew can also get a higher-tier ship through the story: salvage, a reward, a theft, or a debt. Upgrades installed on the old ship can move to the new one during a long rest at a drydock.

Chases and Pursuit

Run a chase with the SRD's linked progress and consequence countdowns. Both advance from the same action rolls.

CountdownStartAt 0
Escape (progress)6You break away, jump to hyperspace, or lose them in the clouds.
Caught (consequence)4You're cornered, tractored, or boarded.

Each maneuver, Plot a Course, or Repair Systems roll advances the countdowns as the SRD's dynamic countdown chart describes:

Roll resultEscapeCaught
Critical SuccessTick down 3—
Success with HopeTick down 2—
Success with FearTick down 1Tick down 1
Failure with Hope—Tick down 2
Failure with Fear—Tick down 3

Speed: If you're faster than your pursuers, start Escape at 5. If you're slower, start Caught at 3.

Chase Complications (d6)

When the GM wants a complication, roll or choose:

d6Complication
1Asteroid field: Each ship must make a Slip Through roll or mark a Hull.
2Debris cloud: Each ship marks a Stress.
3New contact: An enemy flight appears at Far range.
4Gravity well: Afterburn costs an additional Stress until you escape it.
5Flak barrage: Each ship must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll (11) or mark a Shield Slot.
6System glitch: One Critical System fails until repaired.

Hyperspace

Plotting a jump is the Navigator's Knowledge Roll, or an Instinct Roll for a route they've flown before. Adjust the listed time for the ship's Hyperdrive Class.

RouteDifficultyTypical time
Known hyperlane11A short rest
Uncharted or distant14A long rest
Dangerous region17Several long rests
Under fire or near a gravity well+3As above, using an emergency jump
ResultOutcome
Success with HopeYou arrive safely, or early.
Success with FearYou arrive with a complication: the hyperdrive strains (mark a ship Stress), you're followed, or you come out off course.
FailureMisjump: the hyperdrive stalls or drops you somewhere unexpected. The ship marks a Stress, and the GM makes a move.

Emergency jump: To jump under fire, start a progress countdown (4). Successful Pilot, Navigator, or Engineer rolls advance it; at 0, you jump. Interdictors and gravity-well projectors can add a linked consequence countdown.

Boarding

StepWhat happens
1. ClampA Dock and Clamp maneuver, a tractor beam, or a boarding craft brings the ships into Melee range.
2. CountdownStart a Boarding countdown (3). It advances each time the attackers act toward the breach. The defenders can slow it by cutting the clamp (a Pilot's Shake the Tail) or sealing hatches, which the GM can treat as resetting it by 1.
3. BreachAt 0, the boarders are aboard. Switch to personal-scale combat in the Boarding Corridor environment.
4. MeanwhileThe rest of the crew keeps working their stations: the Pilot holds or breaks the clamp, and Engineers and Gunners carry on with their actions.

Running Space Combat

This part is for the GM.

Enemy Ships

Enemy ships use the SRD's adversary stat blocks. Like all adversaries, their damage is a fixed roll, not multiplied by Proficiency. Every enemy ship, sorted by class into fighters, freighters, and capital ships, is in Ship Adversaries.

GM Moves in Space

MoveExample
Spotlight an enemy shipIt closes within Close range and attacks.
Strain the shipThe ship marks a Stress: an engine overheats or a shield flickers.
Introduce a hazardA debris cloud or gravity well appears.
Call reinforcementsSpend a Fear to bring another flight or a shuttle into the scene.
Advance a countdownThe pursuers close in, or the clamp holds.
Use a featureA Star Destroyer's Broadside, or an Ion Storm's Ion Surge.

Running Capital Ship Battles

Two steps of scale turn most hits from fighters into no damage at all, so a squadron can't grind down a Star Destroyer's Hull with ordinary fire. Give the PCs objectives instead: weapons that break the scale rule, such as torpedoes; systems they can target separately, such as shield domes or a bridge; a Target the Flagship countdown; or a ground team. Capital ships fall to plans, not attrition.

Scale works in the players' favor too: a capital ship's guns turn a fighter's Minor hits into Severe ones, so let fighters dodge (Evasive Action, Slow Tracking) rather than trade blows.

Building a Ship

To stat a player ship that isn't in the catalog, start from its tier. Ship thresholds don't add the crew's level, so higher-tier ships have higher thresholds instead, matching a PC's armor and level at that tier.

TierEvasion + HullFighter thresholdsFreighter thresholdsCapital thresholds
115–165/10 to 7/148/16—
216–178/16 to 10/2011/22 to 12/24—
317–1813/2616/32 to 18/36—
418–19——22/45 to 25/50
  • Stress and Shields: fighters have 2–4 Stress and 0–2 Shield Slots; freighters 3–5 and 1–3; capital ships 6–7 and 3–4.
  • Speed and hyperdrive: nimble ships are Fast or Blazing; heavy ones Standard or Slow. Most hyperdrives are Class 1 or 2.
  • Weapons: one or two from Ship Weapons, three for capital ships.
  • Features: one or two, drawn from what the ship does on screen.

Enemy ships use adversary stat blocks instead; see Ship Adversaries.

Asteroid fields, ion storms, trench runs, fleet battles, and other space set pieces have their own environment stat blocks: see Space Environments in the Environments chapter.

Chapter 9

Ground Vehicles

Ground Vehicles

Speeders, swoops, walkers, and gunships. This chapter stands on its own: you don't need the space combat rules to drive a vehicle. It's in three parts: how vehicles work, the vehicle catalog, and running vehicles for the GM.

Vehicles at a Glance

A vehicle is a piece of gear the whole party can ride, with its own sheet. Everyone in a vehicle still acts on their own spotlight, following the SRD's normal spotlight rules.

RuleDetails
ScaleVehicles are Personal scale, like characters and creatures. Characters' weapons harm vehicles normally, and vehicle weapons harm characters normally.
DrivingThe driver acts at the controls: they move the vehicle and make maneuvers with Agility. The Pilot class's features work behind the controls.
GunnersAnyone in a gunner's seat fires the vehicle's weapons, rolling with the weapon's trait.
DamageAttacks roll against the vehicle's Evasion. Compare damage to its thresholds and mark Hull. Mark an Armor Slot to reduce the severity by one threshold.
StressThe vehicle marks Stress when it's pushed. With none left, it marks Hull instead; when it marks its last Stress, it breaks down.
RidersRiders on an open vehicle can be targeted directly. Riders inside an enclosed one can't.
WrecksWhen the vehicle marks its last Hull, the driver chooses a crash move.

The Vehicle Sheet

FieldMeaning
Name and TierWhat the vehicle is and which tier of play it suits.
EvasionThe number attack rolls against the vehicle must meet or beat.
HullThe vehicle's Hit Points, marked by damage severity.
StressStrain on the engine and frame, marked when you push the vehicle.
Armor SlotsMark one to reduce the severity of incoming damage by one threshold, like a character's armor.
Damage ThresholdsMajor and Severe. Unlike a character's, they don't add your level.
SpeedHow far the vehicle moves (see Moving and Fighting).
Weapons and StationsWhat it fires, and who sits where: a driver, and sometimes gunners.
SeatsHow many people it carries, and whether it's open (riders exposed) or enclosed.
FeaturesWhat makes it special.

Keep a vehicle's sheet in the Starship tool: choose "Vehicles" when you add one.

Moving and Fighting

Movement

When the driver is in the spotlight, the vehicle can move up to its Speed's range as part of the driver's action. To go farther, or to move through danger, the driver makes a maneuver.

SpeedMoves as part of an actionIn a chase
SlowWithin Close rangeDisadvantage to escape or catch a faster vehicle
StandardWithin Far range—
FastWithin Far rangeAdvantage to escape or catch a slower vehicle
BlazingWithin Very Far rangeAs Fast

Characters on foot move within Close range as part of an action, or farther with an Agility Roll, so a Slow walker keeps pace with infantry and a speeder leaves them behind. Getting in or out of a vehicle is part of a move; jumping from a moving one takes an Agility Roll.

Who Does What

  • The driver moves the vehicle and makes maneuvers. A driver whose station says "also fires" can attack with the vehicle's weapons instead of making a maneuver.
  • Gunners fire a weapon: Fire or Focus Fire, as on a ship (see Crew Actions). Vehicle weapons roll damage dice equal to the gunner's Proficiency.
  • Passengers act normally. They can attack out of an open vehicle, but not out of an enclosed one unless a feature says so.
  • Anyone with a Tool Kit can make a Field Repair: a Knowledge Roll against the tier's Difficulty (11, 14, 17, 20). On a success, clear a vehicle Stress or fix one breakdown until the end of the scene.

Riders and Passengers

Open vehicles (marked Open in the catalog: speeder bikes, swoops, the AT-RT, the BARC speeder, the cargo skiff) leave their riders exposed. An attacker can target a rider instead of the vehicle, using the rider's Evasion. When an open vehicle takes Severe damage, each rider must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll against the tier's Difficulty or be thrown off, landing within Close range and marking a Stress.

Enclosed vehicles protect everyone inside. Attacks have to go through the vehicle until the riders get out or it's wrecked.

Driving Maneuvers

Drivers use the pilot maneuvers, rolling Agility against an opposing vehicle's or creature's Difficulty, or the tier's Difficulty for hazards. Most work on the ground as written:

ManeuverOn the ground
Evasive ActionYes.
Get on Its TailYes, against another vehicle or a mounted rider.
Shake the TailYes.
AfterburnYes: mark a vehicle Stress to move anywhere within Far range without a roll.
Strafing RunYes, with a weapon the driver can fire.
RamYes, against a vehicle. Against creatures, use Run Them Down.
Slip ThroughYes, through ground hazards: canyons, forests, crowds, and traffic.
Draw FireYes, protecting an allied vehicle or an ally on foot within Close range.
Dock and ClampNo. Use a tow cable, or have riders jump across.

Two maneuvers work only on the ground:

Run Them Down

Driver station · Ground only

Mark a vehicle Stress and drive through a line of creatures to a point within Close range. Make an attack with Agility against each creature in the path. Targets you succeed against take 1d10+3 physical damage, +3 for each tier above Tier 1, and become temporarily Vulnerable. Walkers and other vehicles can't be run down.

Bootlegger Turn

Driver station · Ground only

On a success, spin the vehicle around. Each pursuer within Close range must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll against your roll's result or overshoot: it ends up at Far range and can't attack you until its next spotlight. Gunners aboard have advantage on their next attack against an overshooting pursuer.

Damage, Breakdowns, and Crashes

Taking Damage

  1. Compare the damage to the vehicle's thresholds. Below Major is Minor (1 Hull), Major or more is 2 Hull, and Severe or more is 3 Hull.
  2. Mark an Armor Slot, if one is free, to reduce the severity by one threshold.
  3. Mark the Hull. If it's the vehicle's last Hull, the driver chooses a crash move.

Breakdowns

When a vehicle marks its last Stress, roll a d4 or let the GM choose. The breakdown lasts until it's repaired.

d4BreakdownEffect while broken
1DriveThe vehicle can't move beyond Very Close range.
2WeaponsIts weapons can't attack.
3ControlsThe driver's maneuvers have disadvantage.
4SensorsAttacks from the vehicle beyond Close range have disadvantage.

Crashing

When a vehicle marks its last Hull, the driver chooses one of these. A vehicle is closer to the ground than a starship, so its crashes rarely kill the crew, but they rarely leave them unhurt.

  • Crash Landing: Make an Agility Roll against the tier's Difficulty. On a success, the vehicle grinds to a stop, everyone gets out, and it's out of action until repaired. On a failure, the vehicle is destroyed and everyone aboard marks a Hit Point.
  • Risk It All: Roll your Duality Dice. If the Hope Die is higher, the vehicle holds together and clears Hull equal to the Hope Die's value. If the Fear Die is higher, it's destroyed and everyone aboard marks a Hit Point. If they match, clear all Hull and Stress.

Repairs

WhenRepair
In a sceneA Field Repair (see Who Does What).
Short restPatch Up (downtime move, needs a Tool Kit): Clear 1d4 + your tier in vehicle Stress and Armor Slots, in any combination, or fix one breakdown.
Long restOverhaul (downtime move, needs a Tool Kit): Clear all vehicle Stress and Armor Slots, fix all breakdowns, and clear 1d4 Hull.
GarageSpend credits to clear all Hull: 1 handful per Hull at Tier 1, 2 handfuls at Tier 2, 1 bag at Tier 3, and 2 bags at Tier 4.

Vehicle Weapons

Vehicle weapons roll damage dice equal to the gunner's Proficiency and add +3 flat damage for each tier above Tier 1, using the vehicle's tier. The catalog lists each vehicle's weapons with that bonus already added.

WeaponTraitRangeDamageFeature
Light Blaster CannonAgilityFard6+2 phy—
Laser CannonsAgilityFard8+2 phy—
Repeating Blaster CannonAgilityFard8+3 phyQuick
Concussion Grenade LauncherFinesseFard8+2 phySplash
Mass-Driver CannonStrengthVery Fard12+4 phyPowerful
Missile LauncherFinesseFard10+4 phyLimited (2)
Harpoon and Tow CableFinesseClose—Tow Cable: on a success against a walker's legs, the cable wraps it. On the walker's next move, it trips: it marks 3 Hull and is Vulnerable until the end of the scene. Limited (1).
  • Limited (X): You can fire this weapon X times. It reloads during a rest.
  • Powerful: On a successful attack, roll an additional damage die and discard the lowest result.
  • Quick: When you make an attack, you can mark a vehicle Stress to target another enemy within range.
  • Splash: On a successful attack, you can mark a vehicle Stress to deal half the damage to each other enemy within Very Close range of the target.

Running Vehicles

This part is for the GM.

Stat Block or Vehicle Sheet?

Use an adversary stat block for any vehicle you control, and a vehicle sheet for any vehicle the PCs control. Stat blocks are faster to run and keep your side of the table simple; vehicle sheets give the players stations, Armor Slots, and maneuvers to play with. When the PCs capture an enemy vehicle, switch it to its vehicle sheet and carry over the damage: its HP becomes its Hull.

Enemy Vehicles

Every enemy vehicle is in the Adversaries chapter, with the rest of its faction, and in the Encounter Builder.

VehicleTierRoleUse it for
Swoop Gang1HordeRoad ambushes and chases
Imperial Troop Transport1SupportCity patrols that drop off troopers
AAT Battle Tank2BruiserClone Wars battlefields
Hailfire Droid2RangedLong-range bombardment
TX-225 Occupier Tank2BruiserOccupied cities and convoys
AT-ST2SoloA walker hunting the party
AT-AT3SoloA set-piece battle

Taking Down a Walker

Walkers and tanks have high thresholds, so blaster fire alone rarely brings one down. Give the players other ways in, and reward them for finding one:

  • Weak points. A tank's rear or a walker's neck can ignore its armor, like the AAT's Armored Front. Tell the players when they spot one.
  • Tangle and trip. Cables and logs can Restrain a walker, as on the AT-ST; the T-47's Harpoon and Tow Cable trips one outright.
  • Get aboard. A PC who climbs on can try a Hijack, as on the AT-ST.
  • Ion weapons ignore some armor features, like the TX-225's Armored Hull.
  • Countdowns. For a huge walker like the AT-AT, run a progress countdown to bring it down instead of tracking every hit.

Ground Chases

Run a chase on the ground like one in space: linked Escape (6) and Caught (4) countdowns, advanced by the driver's maneuvers (see Chases and Pursuit). For a ready-made pursuit through traffic or a forest, use the Speeder Chase environment.

Chapter 10

Running an Adventure

Running an Adventure

GM Guidance

GM moves change the story in response to what the players do. They aren't bound to specific abilities: describe them however the fiction demands. A GM turn begins when the spotlight passes to you and ends when it passes back to the players.

GM Principles

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

Begin and End With the Fiction

Use the fiction to drive mechanics, then connect the mechanics back to the fiction.

Collaborate At All Times, Especially During Conflict

The PCs are the protagonists of the campaign; antagonism between player and GM should exist only in the fiction.

Fill the World With Life, Wonder, and Danger

Showcase rich cultures, take the PCs to wondrous places, and introduce them to dangerous creatures.

Ask Questions and Incorporate the Answers

Ensuring that the players’ ideas are included results in a narrative that supports the whole group’s creativity.

Give Every Roll Impact

Only ask the players to roll during meaningful moments.

Play to Find Out What Happens

Be surprised by what the characters do, the choices they make, and the people they become.

Hold on Gently

Don’t worry if you need to abandon or alter something that came before.

GM Practices

Cultivate a Curious Table

Follow what catches the players’ interest to foster an environment of creative inquiry.

Gain Your Players’ Trust

Act in good faith, follow through on your promises, admit your mistakes.

Keep the Story Moving Forward

Advance the story through escalating action, new information, or changing circumstances after every action roll, whether it succeeds or fails.

Cut to the Action

Skip past the boring bits. When a scene drags on, end it.

Help the Players Use the Game

Players have more fun when you help them understand the system.

Create a Meta Conversation

Empower players to speak out of character, use safety tools, and ask for clarification.

Tell Them What They Would Know

Don’t hide obvious details or important information from the players.

Ground the World in Motive

An NPC’s actions flow from their goals and desires.

Bring the Game’s Mechanics to Life

Set a good example of how fiction and mechanics work together to enhance the game experience.

Reframe Rather Than Reject

If a player’s contribution conflicts with the fiction, work with them to reshape it.

Work in Moments and Montages

When framing a scene, decide which beats should be savored and which shouldn’t linger.

Pitfalls to Avoid

Undermining the Heroes

If a roll doesn’t go well, show how it was impacted by an adversary’s prowess, environmental factors, or unexpected surprises, rather than the PC’s incompetence.

Always Telling the Players What to Roll

Let the players decide how to handle a challenge.

Letting Scenes Drag

Shake it up or cut away when a scene has concluded, the table’s energy is flagging, or people are talking in circles.

Singular Solutions

Don’t get hung up on one right answer to a problem. If the players have a clever idea, make it work.

Overplanning

Spend your prep time inventing situations instead of scripting scenes. If the players surprise you, take a break to think through your options.

Hoarding Fear

Spend Fear when you have the opportunity. The players will always generate more.

For more in-depth GM guidance, see pg.

When to Make a Move

Make a GM move when the players:

  • Roll with Fear.

  • Fail an action roll.

  • Do something that has unavoidable consequences, like shooting a stormtrooper in a crowded spaceport.

  • Give you a golden opportunity, like leaving the ship unguarded.

  • Look to you for what happens next.

Choosing Moves by Result

ResultShorthandYour responseStar Wars example
Critical SuccessYes, and moreLet the player describe their success, then give them an extra opportunity or advantage.The slicer opens the door and finds the station's patrol schedule on the same terminal.
Success with HopeYes, andLet the player describe their success, then show how the world reacts.The bluff works; the officer waves you through.
Success with FearYes, butWork with the player to describe the success, take a Fear, and introduce a minor consequence.The ship makes the jump, but the hyperdrive sparks: the ship marks a Stress.
Failure with HopeNo, butDescribe how the PC fails, then make a move introducing a minor consequence.The lock won't budge, and a patrol droid rolls closer.
Failure with FearNo, andDescribe how things go wrong, take a Fear, and make a move introducing a major consequence.The bounty hunter spots you, calls in her partners, and you're cut off from the crew.

Minor consequences: an adversary attacks, the PC marks a Stress, you introduce a new threat, or you raise the stakes.

Major consequences: you put them in immediate danger, they become the focus of multiple adversaries, they're separated from the party, or they lose an important opportunity for good.

Soft and Hard Moves

Soft moves reveal new information and give the party a chance to react. Hard moves are harsher and more direct: the PCs get no opening to interrupt or avoid the outcome. Use softer moves on rolls with Hope and harder moves on rolls with Fear.

Soft moveHard move
A TIE patrol appears on the scanner, still at Very Far range.The TIEs open fire before the crew knows they're there.
The cantina goes quiet as a Gamorrean enforcer looks your way.The enforcer's blaster is already pressed to your back.
The Inquisitor's voice echoes from somewhere above.The Inquisitor drops down and ignites her saber between you and the exit.

Core GM Mechanics

Using Fear

  • You start a campaign with 1 Fear per PC in the party.

  • You gain Fear when a PC rolls with Fear, when the PCs take a rest, or when an ability or effect says so.

  • You can never have more than 12 Fear, and Fear carries over between sessions.

Spend a Fear to interrupt the players and make a move, make an additional GM move, use an adversary's or environment's Fear feature, or add an adversary's Experience to a roll.

SceneStar Wars exampleFear
IncidentalBuying parts in Mos Eisley; a quiet talk aboard the ship; resting in hyperspace.0–1
MinorA speeder ride across the dunes; a skirmish with a scout trooper patrol.1–3
StandardA firefight to reach a hangar; a tense meeting with a crime lord; running a blockade.2–4
MajorA duel with an Inquisitor; a battle against a Star Destroyer; a betrayal by a trusted ally.4–8
ClimacticThe final confrontation with the arc's villain; the assault on a superweapon; a lightsaber duel that decides a PC's fate.6–12

If you have a lot of Fear, consider spending it fast, often, or big. Fear moves often bring in adversaries the players didn't see coming, unleash an adversary's most powerful ability, or turn the environment hard against the party.

Rolling Dice

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

The GM has no Duality Dice; instead, they roll a single d20 called the GM’s Die.

Adversary Attack Rolls

When an adversary attacks a PC, roll your d20 and add the adversary’s attack bonus to the result. If the total meets or beats the target’s Evasion, the attack succeeds; otherwise, the attack fails. On a successful attack, roll the attack’s damage dice to determine how much it deals.

If you roll a natural 20 on an attack, your roll automatically succeeds and you deal extra damage. Roll damage normally, then add the highest number on the damage dice to the total. For example, an attack that deals 3d6+2 deals 18+3d6+2 on a critical success; the critical success does not affect the flat damage modifier. Note: a critical success on an adversary’s reaction roll automatically succeeds, but confers no additional benefit.

Guidance on Action Rolls

After a player describes a move they want to make during the game, you might decide an action roll is necessary to determine how the scene progresses. Use this guide to determine what to present the player, choosing whichever option best fits the situation:

  • Determine whether the roll is necessary, considering the PC’s Experiences or backstory, the pressure they’re acting under, and the possible outcomes.

  • Establish the stakes of an action roll before the player makes it.

  • Communicate any unavoidable consequences.

  • If desired, you can offer the player the opportunity to forgo an action roll in exchange for agreeing to an interesting outcome, cost, or complication.

Difficulty Benchmarks

The Difficulty of an attack roll against an adversary is equal to the adversary’s Difficulty score. The Difficulty of any other action rolls against an adversary is equal to the adversary’s Difficulty score, plus (if applicable) the value of one of the adversary relevant Experience modifiers. When a player makes an action roll without a specified Difficulty, the GM sets the Difficulty according to the totality of the circumstances. Giving Advantage and Disadvantage

To viscerally convey how a PC’s actions or circumstances affect their ability to act, grant them advantage die (or impose disadvantage die) instead of adjusting the Difficulty of an action roll.

Adversary Action Rolls

By default, adversaries don’t normally make action rolls except for attack rolls and any unique actions described in their stat blocks. Any other action an adversary attempts simply succeeds without an action roll; if you want an adversary’s action to have a chance of failure, have any relevant PCs make reaction rolls instead. However, for especially dramatic or difficult tasks that the PCs can’t influence, you can give an adversary an action roll anyway. For an adversary’s action roll, roll a d20. If the result is equal to or greater than the action’s Difficulty, the action succeeds—otherwise it fails. You can spend a Fear before rolling to add a relevant Experience from the adversary’s stat block to the total. Use the same procedure when an adversary makes a reaction roll.

Adversary Advantage & Disadvantage

If an adversary has advantage on an action roll, the GM rolls an extra d20 and counts only the higher result. If an adversary has disadvantage on an action roll, the GM rolls an extra d20 and counts only the lower result.

Adversary Attacks

When an adversary attacks a PC, the GM rolls a d20 and adds the adversary’s Attack Modifier to the result. If the total meets or beats the target’s Evasion, the attack succeeds; otherwise, it fails. Before rolling, the GM can grant the attacking adversary advantage, impose disadvantage, or spend a Fear to add a relevant Experience from the adversary’s stat block to the total.

On a success, the adversary deals the damage listed in their stat block to the target. When an adversary’s action lets the GM make an attack against multiple targets, they make one attack roll and compare it to each target’s Evasion separately.

Countdowns

Countdowns represent a period of time or series of events preceding a future effect. A countdown begins at a starting value. When a countdown advances, it’s reduced by 1. The countdown’s effect is triggered when the countdown reaches 0. Note: You can track countdowns by “spinning down” dice or ticking off boxes.

Standard countdowns advance every time a player makes an action roll. If an adversary or environment ability refers to a “Countdown [n],” then it means a standard countdown with a starting value of n. Dynamic countdowns advance by up to 3 depending on the outcomes of action rolls. Consequence countdowns are dynamic countdowns to negative effects. Progress countdowns are dynamic countdowns to positive effects. Dynamic countdowns advance according to this chart:

Dynamic Countdown Advancement

Roll resultProgress countdownConsequence countdown
Failure with Fear

No advancement

Tick down 3

Failure with Hope

No advancement

Tick down 2

Success with Fear

Tick down 1

Tick down 1

Success with Hope

Tick down 2

No advancement

Critical Success

Tick down 3

No advancement

Advanced Countdown Features

  • Countdowns with randomized starting values

  • Loop countdowns that reset to their starting value after their countdown effect is triggered.

  • Increasing countdowns that increase their starting value by 1 every time they loop.

  • Decreasing countdowns that decrease their starting value by 1 every time they loop.

  • Linked progress and consequence countdowns that simultaneously advance according to the same action roll outcomes.

  • Long-term countdowns that advance after rests instead of action rolls.

Running GM NPCs

When you run NPCs as the GM, you should always strive to follow your GM principles and use them to bring the world to life. Differentiate NPCs with unique manners of speech and action; let their individual goals and desires motivate their actions.

The only essential elements for a NPC are their name,

description, and motive. If it’s likely that the PCs will roll actions against them, give them a Difficulty. Adversaries can be invented or improvised by modifying the stat block of another adversary.

If an NPC becomes an ally in combat, they don’t need a stat block—just put the spotlight on what they do and show how their involvement alters the fiction. If a PC capitalizes on their help during the scene, give the PC advantage. NPCs that don’t have Hit Points or Stress can still be injured or killed if the fiction demands it.

If you want an important NPC to mechanically interact with the system, you can give them one or more features with specific triggers and effects. An NPC might also have a choice that adjusts the parameters of their feature. For example:

Choice: When the battle begins, choose a favored PC.

Trigger: The first time during a battle the favored PC is within Close range and hit with an attack.

Effect: Make an attack roll with a +6 modifier against the adversary. On a success, the target is temporarily Restrained by tendrils of powerful magic.

Optional GM Mechanics

Fate Rolls

When the GM wants to leave an outcome entirely up to chance, they call for a fate roll. The GM establishes what’s at stake and how the roll will be interpreted. Then a player rolls one of their Duality Dice and interprets the result. Examples:

“Roll your Fear Die. On a 4 or lower, the fire spreads beyond this house.”

“I think it’s really up to chance whether reinforcements will make it to you in time. Go ahead and roll your Fear Die—

that’ll determine the starting size of the countdown. When that triggers, reinforcements will arrive in your Far range.”

“Go ahead and roll your Hope Die to see how big the crowd at the cantina is tonight. The higher the roll, the bigger the crowd.”

“Make a roll using your Hope Die to determine the number of stim packs the shop has in stock.”

Falling and Collision Damage

If a character falls to the ground, you can use the following as a guide to determine the damage they take:

  • A fall from Very Close range deals 1d10+3 physical damage.

  • A fall from Close range deals 1d20+5 physical damage.

  • A fall from Far or Very Far range deals 1d100+15 physical damage, or death at the GM’s discretion.

If a character collides with an object or another character at a dangerous speed, they take 1d20+5 direct physical damage.

Moving and Fighting Underwater

By default, attack rolls made while the attacker is underwater have disadvantage.

For creatures that can’t breathe underwater, use a standard countdown (3) to track how long they can hold their breath. Advance the countdown whenever the PC takes an action. In addition if they fail a roll or roll with Fear while underwater, you can spend your GM move to advance it an additional time—or twice, if they rolled a failure with Fear.

Once the countdown ends, the underwater PC must mark a Stress whenever they take an action.

Conflict Between PCs

Sometimes a player might want their character to act against another PC in the scene. Before jumping to rolling dice, discuss the situation with both players to decide how to resolve the conflict. A roll might not be necessary to reach an outcome—but if rolling will be fun for everyone involved, come to a consensus on the terms of the roll, then facilitate the scene according to the results. On an attack roll against a PC, the attacker rolls against the defender’s Evasion, just like an adversary. On any other kind of action roll, the instigator makes an action roll and the target makes a reaction roll. To succeed, the instigator must beat a Difficulty equal to the total value of the reaction roll.

Adversaries and Environments

Using Adversaries

Adversaries use stat blocks: tier and type, description, motives and tactics, Difficulty, damage thresholds, Hit Points, Stress, attack modifier, standard attack, optional Experience, and features (Passives, Actions, and Reactions; features that cost a Fear say so).

TypeRole in a fight

SkulkManeuvers and exploits openings to ambush.

StandardRepresentative of their group.
SupportBoosts allies and disrupts opponents.

Daggerheart SRD rule, unchanged in Kyberheart.

When an adversary marks their last Hit Point, they are defeated: incapacitated, tied up, routed, killed, or anything else the table decides makes sense.

Stormtrooper

Tier 1 Standard

An Imperial soldier in white plastoid armor, one of countless thousands serving the Empire.

Motives & Tactics: Advance in formation, follow orders, pin down, call for backup

Pinning Fire Action Make an attack against a target within Far range. On a success, deal 1d6 physical damage, and the target is temporarily Restrained as they're pinned behind cover.

Sandtrooper

Tier 1 Standard

Motives & Tactics: Patrol the settlements, search every speeder, ride down fugitives

Difficulty: 12 | Thresholds: 6/11 | HP: 4 | Stress: 2

ATK: +0 | E-11 Blaster Rifle: Far | 1d8+2 phy

Experience: Desert Patrol +2

Desert Gear Passive The Sandtrooper ignores penalties and hazards from heat, sand, and sandstorms.

Dewback Rider Passive While mounted on a dewback, the Sandtrooper can move within Far range when spotlighted.

Search the Area Action Spend a Fear. Every hidden PC within Far range of a Sandtrooper must succeed on a Finesse Roll (12) or be found, and the Sandtroopers call it in.

Source: Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope

Stormtrooper Squad

Tier 1 Minion

Rank-and-file troopers who pour into a fight by the dozen.

Motives & Tactics: Overwhelm, surround, die for the Empire

Difficulty: 10 | Thresholds: None | HP: 1 | Stress: 1

ATK: +0 | E-11 Blaster Rifle: Far | 2 phy

Minion (3) Passive The Stormtrooper is defeated when they take any damage. For every 3 damage a PC deals to the Stormtrooper, defeat an additional Minion within range the attack would succeed against.

Group Attack Action Spend a Fear to choose a target and spotlight all Stormtrooper Squad members within Far range of them. Those Minions make one shared attack roll. On a success, they deal 2 physical damage each. Combine this damage.

Source: Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope; Star Wars Rebels

Stormtrooper Sergeant

Tier 1 Leader

A squad leader marked by an orange or black pauldron, barking orders over the comm.

Motives & Tactics: Coordinate the squad, hold the line, call reinforcements

Difficulty: 13 | Thresholds: 7/13 | HP: 6 | Stress: 3

ATK: +2 | E-11 Blaster Rifle: Far | 1d10+3 phy

Experience: Commander +2, Imperial Training +2

Form Up! Action Spend 2 Fear to spotlight the Sergeant and up to 2d4 allies within Far range.

Call for Backup Action Mark a Stress to bring a Stormtrooper Squad, one Minion per PC, into the scene at Far range.

Momentum Reaction When the Sergeant makes a successful attack against a PC, you gain a Fear.

Source: Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope; Star Wars Rebels

Heavy Stormtrooper

Tier 1 Bruiser

A trooper lugging a heavy repeating blaster, built to suppress and shred.

Motives & Tactics: Dig in, suppress, cover the advance

Difficulty: 12 | Thresholds: 7/14 | HP: 7 | Stress: 3

ATK: +1 | DLT-19 Heavy Blaster: Far | 1d12+3 phy

Experience: Heavy Weapons +2

Reinforced Armor Passive When the Heavy Stormtrooper takes physical damage, reduce it by 2.

Braced Position Passive While the Heavy Stormtrooper hasn't moved this scene, its attack rolls gain a +2 bonus.

Suppressing Fire Action Mark a Stress to make an attack against all targets within Very Close range of a point within Far range. Targets the Heavy succeeds against take 1d8+2 physical damage.

Source: Star Wars: Episode IV A New Hope; Star Wars Battlefront II (2017)

Mudtrooper Squad

Tier 1 Minion

Mud-caked Imperial infantry grinding through the trenches of Mimban and other conquered worlds.

Motives & Tactics: Hold the trench, advance in waves, follow orders

Difficulty: 10 | Thresholds: None | HP: 1 | Stress: 1

ATK: +0 | Blaster Rifle: Far | 3 phy

Minion (4) Passive The Mudtrooper is defeated when it takes any damage. For every 4 damage a PC deals to the Mudtrooper, defeat an additional Minion within range the attack would succeed against.

Group Attack Action Spend a Fear to choose a target and spotlight all Mudtroopers within Close range of them. Those Minions move within Far range of the target and make one shared attack roll. On a success, they deal 3 physical damage each. Combine this damage.

Trench Fighters Passive While in mud, trenches, or swamp, attacks against Mudtroopers from Far range have disadvantage.

Source: Solo: A Star Wars Story

Scout Trooper

Tier 1 Skulk

A lightly armored trooper who patrols the frontier on a speeder bike and strikes from cover.

Motives & Tactics: Patrol, track, report, strike from hiding

Difficulty: 13 | Thresholds: 5/10 | HP: 4 | Stress: 3

ATK: +2 | Scout Blaster Pistol: Close | 1d6+3 phy

Experience: Recon +3, Stealth +2

Speeder Bike Passive While mounted, the Scout Trooper can move anywhere within Very Far range when spotlighted, and attacks against it from Far range or beyond have disadvantage.

Out of Nowhere Passive The Scout Trooper has advantage on attacks while Hidden.

Spotter Action Mark a Stress to mark a target within Far range for the squad. The target becomes temporarily Vulnerable.

Source: Star Wars: Episode VI Return of the Jedi; Rogue One: A Star Wars Story; The Mandalorian

Shoretrooper

Tier 1 Standard

A coastal garrison trooper guarding tropical Imperial installations like the data vault on Scarif.

Motives & Tactics: Guard the perimeter, take cover, call in heavy weapons

Difficulty: 12 | Thresholds: 7/13 | HP: 4 | Stress: 2

ATK: +1 | Heavy Blaster Rifle: Far | 1d10+3 phy

Garrison Discipline Passive While the Shoretrooper is in cover, attacks against it have disadvantage.

Call the Tank Action Once per scene, spend a Fear to bring an AT-DP or similar Tier 2 Bruiser into the scene at Very Far range.

Source: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story

Snowtrooper

Tier 1 Standard

A cold-weather stormtrooper with a life-support backpack and a heated suit, built for ice worlds.

Motives & Tactics: Advance through snow, set up E-Web guns, escort walkers

Difficulty: 11 | Thresholds: 7/12 | HP: 4 | Stress: 2

ATK: +1 | Blaster Rifle: Far | 1d8+3 phy

Cold-Weather Gear Passive The Snowtrooper ignores penalties and hazards from cold, snow, and ice.

E-Web Emplacement Action Spend a Fear for two Snowtroopers within Very Close range of each other to set up a heavy repeating blaster. Until they move, each spotlight they can attack every target in a line out to Far range. Targets they succeed against take 1d12+4 physical damage.

Source: Star Wars: Episode V The Empire Strikes Back

Death Trooper

Tier 2 Standard

An elite trooper in black armor, speaking in garbled code, assigned to Imperial Intelligence's deadliest missions.

Motives & Tactics: Move silently, protect the director, eliminate witnesses

ATK: +3 | E-11D Blaster Rifle: Far | 2d8+4 phy

Experience: Special Operations +3

Out of Nowhere Passive The Death Trooper has advantage on attacks while Hidden.

Concussion Grenade Action Mark a Stress to throw a grenade at a point within Far range. Each creature within Very Close range of it must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll (14) or take 2d6+3 physical damage and be knocked back to Close range.

Fire Team Reaction When another Death Trooper within Close range deals damage to a creature, you can mark a Stress to make a standard attack against that same creature. On a success, combine the damage.

Momentum Reaction When the Death Trooper makes a successful attack against a PC, you gain a Fear.

Source: Rogue One: A Star Wars Story; Star Wars Rebels; The Mandalorian

Elite Squad Trooper

Tier 2 Ranged

A hand-picked Imperial marksman sent on missions too delicate for regular stormtroopers.

Motives & Tactics: Pick off targets, cover the squad, follow the mission to the letter

ATK: +3 | Precision Rifle: Very Far | 2d10+4 phy

Experience: Marksmanship +3

Steady Aim Action Mark a Stress to aim at a target within Very Far range. Its next attack against them has advantage and deals an extra 1d8 damage.

Suppressing Fire Action Spend a Fear. Each PC within Close range of a point within Far range must mark a Stress or move out of the area.

Source: Star Wars: The Bad Batch

Incinerator Trooper

Tier 2 Bruiser

A stormtrooper carrying a flamethrower, used to burn out villages and clear buildings.

Motives & Tactics: Burn, clear cover, flush targets out, intimidate

ATK: +2 | Flamethrower: Close | 2d10+4 phy

Gout of Flame Action Mark a Stress to spray fire in a cone. Each creature in front of the trooper within Close range must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll (14) or take 2d10+4 physical damage and catch fire, marking a Stress at the start of each GM turn until they spend an action to put it out.

Fuel Tank Reaction When the Incinerator Trooper takes Severe damage, its tank ruptures. Each creature within Very Close range must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll (14) or take 2d8+3 physical damage.

Source: The Mandalorian

Night Trooper Legion

Tier 2 Horde (2/HP)

Stormtroopers of Thrawn's Seventh Legion, kept fighting long past death by Nightsister magick.

Difficulty: 14 | Thresholds: 10/20 | HP: 6 | Stress: 3

ATK: +2 | Blaster Rifles: Far | 2d8+3 phy

Horde (1d10+2) Passive When the Legion has marked half or more of its HP, its standard attack deals 1d10+2 physical damage instead.

Deathless Passive The Legion never marks Stress from fear, intimidation, or Presence effects.

Rise Again Reaction The first time the Legion is defeated in a scene, spend a Fear to have it clear 3 Hit Points as the fallen troopers stand back up.

Source: Ahsoka

Purge Trooper

Tier 2 Bruiser

An elite trooper in black armor trained for one purpose: killing Jedi.

Difficulty: 14 | Thresholds: 12/24 | HP: 7 | Stress: 4

ATK: +1 | Electrostaff: Very Close | 2d10+4 phy

Experience: Jedi Hunter +3

Anti-Jedi Training Passive When the Purge Trooper takes magic damage, reduce it by 4.

Spinning Staff Action Mark a Stress to make an attack against all targets within Very Close range. Targets the Purge Trooper succeeds against take 2d8+3 physical damage.

Shock Discharge Reaction When a creature within Melee range deals damage to the Purge Trooper, mark a Stress to make that creature mark a Stress.

Variants: Electrobaton troopers trade Spinning Staff for Baton Flurry Action make two standard attacks against one target. Hammer troopers trade it for Ground Slam Action mark a Stress; each creature within Very Close range must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll (14) or take 2d10+2 physical damage and be knocked back to Close range.

Source: Star Wars Jedi: Fallen Order; Obi-Wan Kenobi

Range Trooper

Tier 2 Skulk

A rugged stormtrooper with magnetic boots, fighting on the outside of speeding trains and starships.

Difficulty: 14 | Thresholds: 9/18 | HP: 5 | Stress: 3

ATK: +2 | Blaster Rifle: Far | 2d8+3 phy

Mag Boots Passive The Range Trooper can walk on walls, hulls, and the outside of moving vehicles and can't be knocked back.

Uncouple Action Spend a Fear to cut a cable, release a car, or blow a coupling within Close range. Anyone on the separated section must succeed on an Agility Reaction Roll (14) or fall or be left behind.

Tier 1 Social

An Imperial Security Bureau officer with a soft voice, a datapad full of files, and the power to make people disappear.

Experience: Interrogation +3, Imperial Bureaucracy +2

I Know Who You Are Action Once per scene, mark a Stress to reveal one fact a PC has tried to hide, such as a real name, a past crime, or a rebel contact.

Veiled Threat Action Spend a Fear. A target who can hear the Agent must make a Presence Reaction Roll (13). On a failure, they mark 2 Stress or answer one question truthfully.

Call It In Reaction When the Agent is attacked, mark a Stress to bring a Stormtrooper Squad, one Minion per PC, into the scene at Far range.

Worth More Alive Passive The Scientist knows something the PCs need. They mark a Stress instead of a Hit Point the first time they would be defeated, then surrender.
