The Inciting Incident

You can use the prompt below to start your campaign, or create your own.

In 1 BBY, Jedha City lives under Imperial occupation. Star Destroyers hang over the holy city while kyber crystals are hauled off-world by the ton, and Saw Gerrera's Partisans ambush patrols in the streets.

Teva Ossin (she/her), a rebel handler who never stays in one place for long, has a job. Lieutenant Corin Hask (he/him), an Imperial logistics officer on Jedha, wants to defect. He says he has shipping records showing where the kyber is really going, and he'll trade them for safe passage off-world. Teva can't send her own people; the ISB is watching them. She needs a crew no one knows.

The catch: ISB Supervisor Delle Varkas (she/her) already suspects Hask, and she's set a trap to catch whoever comes for him. Saw's Partisans want Hask's records for themselves and don't trust anyone else to use them. And Hask may not be telling the truth about what he knows, or about why he's running.

Character hooks:

  • Force Adepts feel something wrong on Jedha: thousands of kyber crystals crying out as they're taken.

  • Soldiers and Imperial Academy characters may know Hask from training, or know the trap Varkas is setting.

  • Scoundrels, Pilots, and Bounty Hunters are offered real credits, and a ship to get off Jedha with.

  • Operatives and Consulars might already be part of Teva's network, or owe her a favor.

Other starting points:

  • The Purge (19 BBY): A clone squad that removed their inhibitor chips is sheltering a Jedi youngling, and an Inquisitor is closing in.

  • The Dark Times (10 BBY): The Path asks the crew to smuggle a Force-sensitive child off-world before the Inquisitors arrive.

  • The Galactic Civil War (3 ABY): After the Battle of Hoth, a scattered rebel cell needs supplies, and the only crew willing to run the blockade has a price on its head.

Campaign Mechanics

The following mechanics are unique to this campaign.

Imperial Heat

Imperial Heat measures how much attention the Empire is paying to the party. It's a shared track from 0 to 6, kept where everyone can see it.

Gaining Heat. The GM marks 1 Heat when the party:

  • Leaves witnesses or evidence of a crime against the Empire.

  • Uses the Force or a lightsaber where Imperials can see.

  • Uses real names or identities after they're Wanted.

  • Fails with Fear on a roll to avoid Imperial notice.

The GM marks 2 Heat for a major blow against the Empire done in the open, such as raiding a garrison or destroying an Imperial ship.

Effects. At the start of each session, the GM gains Fear equal to half the party's Heat, rounded down. Heat also has two thresholds:

  • Wanted (3+): Bounties are posted. Imperial checkpoints treat the PCs as if they're on a Wanted Bulletin, and bounty hunters may come calling.

  • Hunted (6): The Empire assigns a dedicated hunter, such as an Inquisitor, an ISB Agent, or an Elite Bounty Hunter. They become a recurring adversary, and Heat can't drop below 3 until the party defeats, deceives, or truly escapes them.

Losing Heat. The party can lower Heat in these ways:

  • Lay Low: During a long rest, a PC can choose this downtime move to clear 1 Heat, or 2 with a safe house or a trusted contact. Only one PC can Lay Low per rest.

  • New Identities: Buying forged Imperial IDs for the whole crew (1 bag of credits) clears 2 Heat.

  • Change Sectors: Jumping to a different sector clears 1 Heat. This works once per sector.

The Pull of the Dark Side

The dark side is quick and seductive, and it leaves a mark. Any PC can be tempted, not just Force Adepts.

Darkness tokens. A PC gains a Darkness token and places it on their character sheet when they:

  • Use the Force to harm someone out of anger, hatred, or fear. The player and GM decide together whether an act counts.

  • Draw power from a Sith holocron, dark side relic, or dark side nexus.

  • Do something cruel or merciless that their character knows is wrong.

Falling. When a PC gains a Darkness token, they roll their Fear Die. If the result is equal to or lower than the number of Darkness tokens on their sheet, the dark side takes hold: they gain a scar and clear all their Darkness tokens. Describe how the dark side marks them, such as yellowed eyes, a colder voice, or a cruelty they can't take back.

Sith. PCs with the Sith subclass embrace this power. When they gain a Darkness token, they also gain a Hope, but they still roll to see if they fall.

Redemption. Darkness tokens don't clear on their own. A PC can clear 1 token at the end of a session by describing a moment that session when they chose compassion or mercy over power. Characters from the Jedi Order community can also clear 1 token during a long rest by meditating as a downtime move.

Forged Imperial IDs

Forged IDs are uncommon items costing 3 handfuls of credits each. A character carrying one has advantage on rolls to pass Imperial inspections, such as the Spaceport Docking Bay's Papers, Please and the Imperial Checkpoint's Scan and Search. When one of those rolls succeeds with Fear, the ID is burned. It no longer works, and the party marks 1 Heat.

Session Zero Questions

Ask any of these questions to your players, or make your own.

  • Where was your character when the Republic became the Empire, and what did they lose that day?

  • What small act of defiance has your character already committed, and who saw it?

  • Who in your character's life serves the Empire, and how does your character feel about them?

  • What does your character believe will happen to the galaxy if no one fights back?

  • If your character can feel the Force, what was the first sign, and who knows?

  • Which canon events should happen exactly as they do on screen, and which might our story touch?

  • Will the party ever work for the Empire, or for criminals who do? Where is the party's line?

  • How graphic should Imperial violence and atrocities be at our table, and are any topics off-limits?

Campaign Map

Use the canon galaxy map, divided into the Deep Core, Core Worlds, Colonies, Inner Rim, Expansion Region, Mid Rim, Outer Rim, Wild Space, and Unknown Regions. During session zero, have each player mark their character's homeworld and one place the Empire has hurt them. Add the party's ship's usual routes and safe houses as the campaign goes on.

Chapter 15

Appendix

Appendix

Quick references for the table: the core rules on one page, every term in the game, and when your story happens in the galaxy’s history.

Quick Reference

The rules you reach for most at the table, on one page. It summarizes the Daggerheart SRD’s core rules and what Kyberheart adds; the full chapters win if anything differs.

The Duality Dice

Roll a Hope d12 and a Fear d12, add a trait and any modifiers, and compare the total to the Difficulty. If the dice match, it’s a critical success.

ResultWhat happens
Critical success (the dice match)You succeed with a bonus, gain a Hope, and clear a Stress. A critical attack adds the damage dice’s maximum to the damage roll.
Success with HopeYou succeed and gain a Hope.
Success with FearYou succeed with a cost or complication, and the GM gains a Fear.
Failure with HopeYou fail with a minor consequence and gain a Hope, then the spotlight swings to the GM.
Failure with FearYou fail with a major consequence and the GM gains a Fear, then the spotlight swings to the GM.

Difficulty by Tier

A typical Difficulty for hazards and opposition at each tier. Easier and harder tasks move a few points either way.

TierLevelsTypical Difficulty
Tier 1Level 111
Tier 2Levels 2–414
Tier 3Levels 5–717
Tier 4Levels 8–1020

Hope

You can hold up to 6 Hope. Spend it to:

  • Use an Experience: 1 Hope each: add the Experience’s modifier to a roll.
  • Help an Ally: 1 Hope: roll a d6 advantage die and add it to an ally’s action roll. If several allies help, they use the highest die.
  • Tag Team Roll: 3 Hope, once per session: you and an ally both make action rolls, then choose one result to apply to both.
  • Hope Feature: 3 Hope: use your class’s Hope Feature.

Advantage and Disadvantage

  • Advantage: Roll a d6 and add it to your total.
  • Disadvantage: Roll a d6 and subtract it from your total.
  • Both: Advantage and disadvantage dice cancel one for one. Two sources of advantage on your own roll still give one d6, but an ally’s Help an Ally die adds on top.
  • Reaction rolls: Rolls to resist or avoid an effect. They don’t generate Hope or Fear, and a critical success ignores the effect but doesn’t clear Stress or give Hope.

Damage and Hit Points

Compare damage to your thresholds and mark Hit Points. Your thresholds already include your level.

DamageMark
Below your Major threshold (Minor)1 Hit Point
Major threshold or more2 Hit Points
Severe threshold or more3 Hit Points
Double your Severe threshold or more (optional massive damage rule)4 Hit Points

Armor and Stress

  • Armor Slots: Mark one Armor Slot to reduce incoming damage by one threshold, such as Severe to Major. One slot per hit.
  • Stress: When you must mark Stress but have none left, mark a Hit Point instead. You can’t use a move that costs Stress while all your Stress is marked.
  • Last Stress: When you mark your last Stress, you’re Vulnerable until you clear at least one.

Death Moves

When you mark your last Hit Point, choose one:

  • Blaze of Glory: Take one final action. It automatically critically succeeds (with GM approval), then your character dies.
  • Avoid Death: You drop unconscious until an ally clears one of your Hit Points or the party finishes a long rest. Roll your Hope Die: if it’s equal to or lower than your level, you gain a scar.
  • Risk It All: Roll your Duality Dice. Hope higher: clear Hit Points or Stress equal to the Hope Die. Fear higher: your character dies. Matching: clear all Hit Points and Stress.

Range

Ranges describe the space between things. In space, the same names apply to ships.

RangeOn the groundIn space
MeleeWithin reachDocked or colliding
Very CloseAbout 5 to 10 feetA tight dogfight
CloseAbout 10 to 30 feetTypical weapons range
FarAbout 30 to 100 feetLong-range fire
Very FarAbout 100 to 300 feetSensor range

Conditions

  • Hidden: Out of sight, in cover, or off sensors. Rolls against you have disadvantage.
  • Restrained: Held in place by bonds, a net, a tractor beam, or a docking clamp. You can’t move, but you can still act.
  • Vulnerable: Exposed or locked on. Rolls against you have advantage.

Rests and Downtime

On a short rest (about an hour), choose two downtime moves; on a long rest (several hours), choose two of the long versions. You can choose the same move twice. After three short rests in a row, the next rest must be a long rest.

MoveShort restLong rest
Tend to WoundsClear 1d4 + tier Hit Points (you or an ally)Clear all Hit Points
Clear StressClear 1d4 + tier StressClear all Stress
Repair ArmorClear 1d4 + tier Armor SlotsClear all Armor Slots
PrepareGain a Hope, or 2 Hope if you Prepare with othersSame
Work on a Project—Advance a long-term project
Repair Droid (Kyberheart)With a Tool Kit, clear 1d4 Stress on a droidSame
Patch Up (Kyberheart)With a Tool Kit, clear 1d4 + tier ship Stress and Shield Slots, or fix a Critical System—
Overhaul (Kyberheart)—With a Tool Kit, clear all ship Stress and Shields, fix all Critical Systems, and clear 1d4 Hull
Craft (Kyberheart)With a loot formula and its components, craft a consumableSame

The GM’s Fear

The GM can hold up to 12 Fear.

  • Gain Fear: When a player rolls with Fear; 1d4 Fear on a short rest; 1d4 + the number of PCs on a long rest; 1d6 per PC across extended downtime.
  • Spend Fear: To interrupt and make a move, spotlight more adversaries, use an adversary’s or environment’s Fear Feature, or add an adversary’s Experience to a roll.

Space Combat at a Glance

Ships use the same rules as characters. Full rules are in Starships and Space Combat.

  • Damage: Compare to the ship’s thresholds and mark Hull: 1 for Minor, 2 for Major, 3 for Severe.
  • Shields: Mark a Shield Slot to reduce incoming damage by one threshold.
  • Ship Stress: System strain from pushing the ship. With none left, mark Hull instead. The last Stress knocks out a Critical System.
  • Scale: Personal, Fighter, Freighter, Capital. A smaller attacker drops the damage one threshold per step of difference; a larger one raises it.
  • Ship death moves: When a ship marks its last Hull, the pilot chooses Blaze of Glory, Crash Landing, or Risk It All.

Credits

  • Exchange: 10 handfuls make a bag, and 10 bags make a chest.

Glossary

Every term a player or GM might need: Daggerheart’s rules, what Kyberheart adds, and the Star Wars galaxy’s places, groups, gear, and slang.

ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWX

A

ABY / BBY

Star Wars

After and Before the Battle of Yavin, when the first Death Star was destroyed. Galactic dates are counted from it: Order 66 is 19 BBY, and the Battle of Endor is 4 ABY.

Access and Trace

Kyberheart rule

The linked progress and consequence countdowns of a deep slice. When Access reaches 0 the slicer is in; when Trace reaches 0 the system catches them.

See Deep Slices

Action Roll

Daggerheart rule

A roll you make when what your character attempts is risky or difficult. Roll the Duality Dice, add a trait and any modifiers, and compare the total to the Difficulty.

See Action Rolls

Advancement

Daggerheart rule

A permanent improvement chosen when you level up: you take two each level, from options with a free slot in your tier or below, like +1 to two traits, an extra Hit Point slot, or +1 Proficiency.

See Leveling Up

Advantage

Daggerheart rule

Roll a d6 and add it to your total. Disadvantage works the same way but subtracts the d6. If you have both, they cancel out; advantage doesn’t stack.

See Advantage & Disadvantage

Adversary

Daggerheart rule

Any NPC that opposes the party in a fight or conflict, from a stormtrooper to a krayt dragon. Each has a stat block with a tier, a role, Difficulty, thresholds, HP, Stress, an attack, and features.

See Adversaries

Adversary Roles

Daggerheart rule

What an adversary does in a fight: Bruiser (tough, hits hard), Horde (a group acting as one), Leader (commands others), Minion (drops to any damage), Ranged, Skulk (sneaky, mobile), Social, Solo (a fight on its own), Standard, and Support. Roles also set Battle Point costs.

See Adversaries

Armor Score

Daggerheart rule

How many Armor Slots your armor gives you. Some features, like a shield’s Barrier, raise it.

See Armor

Armor Slot

Daggerheart rule

When you take damage, you can mark an Armor Slot to reduce the damage’s severity by one threshold (Severe becomes Major, Major becomes Minor, Minor becomes nothing). You clear them by repairing armor during rests.

See Hit Points & Damage Thresholds

Astromech Droid

Star Wars

A small repair and navigation droid that plugs into starships, like R2-D2 or BD-1. Astromechs speak in beeps and whistles.

See Droid Frames

Attack Roll

Daggerheart rule

An action roll to hit a target, using your weapon’s trait. Against an adversary you need to meet or beat its Difficulty; adversaries attacking you must meet or beat your Evasion.

See Attack Rolls

Attuning a Crystal

Kyberheart rule

A downtime project to bond with a kyber crystal (a countdown of 3 for a Force Adept, 6 for anyone else). An attuned crystal reveals its color, and lets a non–Force Adept wield Force weapons.

See Attuning a Crystal

Aurebesh

Star Wars

The written alphabet of Galactic Basic. The decorative script throughout this site is Aurebesh.

B

Bacta

Star Wars

A healing gel used in patches and bacta tanks to treat wounds quickly.

See Consumables

Bantha Poodoo

Slang & languages

Huttese for bantha dung, meaning garbage or worthless.

Basic (Galactic Basic)

Star Wars

The common language of the galaxy, spoken by most humans and understood by most species.

Battle Points

Daggerheart rule

The GM’s budget for building a fair fight: (3 × the number of PCs) + 2, adjusted for an easier or harder fight. Each adversary costs points by role.

See Encounter Builder

Beskar

Star Wars

Mandalorian iron, prized for armor because it can turn aside blaster bolts and even lightsaber strikes.

See Armor

Binary

Slang & languages

The beeping, whistling language of astromechs and many other droids, also called Droidspeak. Organics can learn to understand it but not speak it.

See Galactic Languages

Black Sun

Star Wars

A powerful criminal syndicate with reach across the galaxy, run by a council of Vigos.

Blaster

Star Wars

The galaxy’s standard firearm, firing bolts of energy. Comes in pistols, rifles, carbines, and heavy repeaters.

See Primary Weapons

Bleeding a Crystal

Kyberheart rule

A dark side ritual that forces a kyber crystal to obey by pouring hatred into it until it turns red. It costs Stress each time, or a Darkness token in The Dark Times.

See Kyber Crystals and Lightsabers

Bocce

Slang & languages

A trade language common among spacers and merchants.

See Galactic Languages

Bounty Hunter

Star Wars

Someone paid to capture or kill a target, often through a guild or a crime lord. Kyberheart has both a Bounty Hunter class and bounty hunter adversaries.

See Bounty Hunter

Bounty Puck

Star Wars

A small holoprojector issued with a bounty, showing the target, the terms, and the reward.

See Bounty Hunting

Burden

Daggerheart rule

Whether a weapon takes one hand or two. You can wield a two-handed primary weapon, or a one-handed primary plus a secondary.

See Equipment Rules

C

Cantina

Star Wars

A bar, usually loud, crowded, and full of spacers and trouble, like the one at Mos Eisley.

Carbonite

Star Wars

A metal used to freeze gas for shipping, and sometimes people. Han Solo was frozen in it.

Cheunh

Slang & languages

The language of the Chiss, rarely taught to outsiders.

See Galactic Languages

Chuba

Slang & languages

Huttese for “you” or “what?”, often said with suspicion.

Class Cards

Kyberheart rule

Kyberheart’s version of Daggerheart’s domain cards: each class has its own deck of Abilities, Spells, and Grimoires, from level 1 to 10.

See Class Cards

Class Feature

Daggerheart rule

An ability every member of a class has, listed in the class entry alongside its Hope feature.

See Classes

Clone Trooper

Star Wars

A soldier of the Galactic Republic, grown on Kamino from the template of the bounty hunter Jango Fett. Clones fought the Clone Wars and were replaced by stormtroopers in the years after Order 66.

See Clone Trooper

Clone Wars

Star Wars

The war between the Galactic Republic and the Separatists (22–19 BBY), fought with clone troopers and battle droids. It ended with Order 66.

Comlink

Star Wars

A handheld or wrist-worn communicator.

See Utility Items

Command (Droid)

Kyberheart rule

To have your droid companion act, make a Spellcast Roll. Guardians and Soldiers use Instinct or Knowledge instead, since they have no Spellcast trait.

See Rules at a Glance

Conditions

Daggerheart rule

Temporary states that change how a creature acts or is targeted. The standard three are Hidden, Restrained, and Vulnerable.

See Conditions

Contraband

Kyberheart rule

Cargo that's restricted or illegal where the crew is flying, like spice, coaxium, or Rebel weapons.

See Contraband

Core Worlds

Star Wars

The wealthy, crowded worlds at the heart of the galaxy, including Coruscant, Corellia, and Alderaan.

Coruscant

Star Wars

The city-covered capital of the Republic and then the Empire, which renamed it Imperial Center.

Countdown

Daggerheart rule

A die or tracker the GM sets to a number and ticks down toward an event, like reinforcements arriving or a reactor exploding. Dynamic countdowns tick by roll results: progress countdowns on successes, consequence countdowns on failures.

See Countdowns

Credit Chips

Kyberheart rule

An optional finer denomination of credits, worth about 10 credits each. Ten chips make a handful.

See Counting Credits

Credits

Kyberheart rule

Money in Kyberheart, counted like Daggerheart’s gold: 10 handfuls make a bag, 10 bags make a chest, and you can hold one chest at most.

See Credit Economy

Crimson Dawn

Star Wars

A criminal syndicate secretly run from the shadows during the Imperial Era; Qi’ra led it in public after Dryden Vos.

Critical Success

Daggerheart rule

When both Duality Dice show the same number. You succeed no matter the total, gain a Hope, and clear a Stress. On an attack, it’s critical damage: add the maximum value of your damage dice to the roll.

See Critical Damage

Critical Systems

Kyberheart rule

When a starship marks its last Stress, one system fails until repaired: Engines, Weapons, Shields, Sensors, Life Support, or Hyperdrive.

See Critical Systems

Cross-Training

Kyberheart rule

At character creation, you can trade one starting class card for a level 1 card from another class’s deck, without gaining that class’s features.

See Cross-Training

D

Damage Thresholds

Daggerheart rule

Two numbers, Major and Severe, that turn damage into Hit Points. Below Major, mark 1 HP (Minor). At or above Major, mark 2. At or above Severe, mark 3. A character’s thresholds come from their armor plus their level.

See Hit Points & Damage Thresholds

Dank Farrik

Slang & languages

A Mandalorian curse, used in frustration.

Dark Side

Star Wars

The aspect of the Force fed by fear, anger, and hatred. It gives quick power but corrupts those who use it.

See The Pull of the Dark Side

The Dark Times

Kyberheart rule

Kyberheart’s campaign frame, set between Order 66 (19 BBY) and the Battle of Endor (4 ABY), with rules for the Jedi Purge, Imperial Heat, and the pull of the dark side.

See The Dark Times

Darkness Token

Kyberheart rule

In The Dark Times, you gain one for using the Force in anger, drawing on dark side relics, or acting cruelly. Each time you gain one, roll your Fear Die: if it’s equal to or lower than your tokens, the dark side takes hold and you gain a scar.

See The Pull of the Dark Side

Darksaber

Star Wars

An ancient black-bladed lightsaber that symbolizes leadership of Mandalore.

Datapad

Star Wars

A handheld computer for reading, notes, maps, and messages.

See Utility Items

Death Moves

Daggerheart rule

When a PC marks their last Hit Point, they choose one: Blaze of Glory (one last heroic action, then death), Avoid Death (fall unconscious and maybe gain a scar), or Risk It All (roll the Duality Dice to live or die).

See Death

Death Star

Star Wars

The Empire’s moon-sized battle station, able to destroy a planet. The first was destroyed at Yavin, the second at Endor.

Debt

Kyberheart rule

Credits owed to a crime lord, syndicate, or client. Once per session the GM can bring it in as a complication, and each PC who owes it gains a Hope.

See Debts

Difficulty

Daggerheart rule

The number an action roll must meet or beat to succeed. Adversaries have their own Difficulty for attacks against them.

See Difficulty Benchmarks

Dosh

Slang & languages

The language of the Trandoshans.

See Galactic Languages

Downtime

Daggerheart rule

What happens during a rest. On a short rest you choose two downtime moves, like tending wounds, clearing Stress, repairing armor, or preparing. On a long rest you can choose bigger ones, like fully recovering or working on a project. The GM gains Fear when the party rests.

See Resting and Downtime Moves

Droid

Star Wars

A robot built for a purpose: astromechs, protocol droids, battle droids, labor droids, and more. Many worlds treat droids as property, and some fit them with restraining bolts.

See Droid

Droid Companion

Kyberheart rule

A loyal droid that travels with your character, using Daggerheart’s Ranger companion rules. It has Evasion, Stress, two Experiences, an attack, a frame, and upgrades, and acts when you command it.

See Droid Companions

Droid Frame

Kyberheart rule

A droid companion’s body type, like Astromech, Protocol, or Heavy. The frame sets its Evasion and Stress and gives it a Frame Feature.

See Droid Frames

Duality Dice

Daggerheart rule

The two twelve-sided dice used for action rolls: one is the Hope Die and one is the Fear Die. Whichever rolls higher decides whether you roll “with Hope” or “with Fear.”

See Action Rolls

Durese

Slang & languages

The language of the Duros.

See Galactic Languages

E

Empire, Galactic

Star Wars

The authoritarian government Palpatine declared at the end of the Clone Wars, ruling through fear, stormtroopers, and its fleet of Star Destroyers.

Environment

Daggerheart rule

A stat block for a place or situation, like a crowded cantina or an asteroid field. Environments have a type (Exploration, Social, Traversal, or Event), a Difficulty, impulses, and features the GM can use.

See Environments

Escape and Caught

Kyberheart rule

The two linked countdowns in a chase: Escape (progress, starting at 6) and Caught (consequence, starting at 4). Whichever reaches 0 first decides the chase.

See Chases and Pursuit

Evasion

Daggerheart rule

The number an adversary’s attack roll must meet or beat to hit you. It starts with your class and changes with armor and advancements.

See Evasion

Ewokese

Slang & languages

The language of the Ewoks of Endor's forest moon.

See Galactic Languages

Experience

Daggerheart rule

A word or phrase describing something your character is good at, like “Smuggler” or “Never Tell Me the Odds.” Spend a Hope to add its bonus (starting at +2) to a roll it applies to.

See Step 7: Create Your Experiences

F

Fate Roll

Daggerheart rule

An optional GM tool: roll one Duality Die to let chance decide something outside the characters’ control, like whether a guard is asleep.

See Fate Rolls

Fear

Daggerheart rule

The GM’s resource, up to 12. The GM gains a Fear whenever a player rolls with Fear, and spends Fear to make moves, interrupt, spotlight adversaries again, and use powerful features.

See Fear

Force Weapon

Kyberheart rule

A weapon powered by the Force, like a lightsaber. Only Force Adepts, or a character who has attuned a kyber crystal, can wield one, and each counts as a lightsaber for features.

See The Force and Damage Types

Force, The

Kyberheart rule

In Kyberheart, only the Force deals magic damage, and only Force Adepts wield it. Force Adept spells and Force weapons deal magic damage; everything else is physical.

See The Force and Damage Types

Force, the

Star Wars

An energy field created by all living things that binds the galaxy together. Force-sensitives can feel and use it; the Jedi follow its light side and the Sith its dark side.

See The Force and Damage Types

G

Galactic Republic

Star Wars

The democratic government that ruled the galaxy for a thousand generations, until Palpatine turned it into the Empire.

GM Move

Daggerheart rule

Something the GM does to push the story: a soft move sets up danger the players can react to; a hard move follows through with a consequence. The GM makes a move whenever a player rolls with Fear or fails.

See GM Guidance

Group Action Roll

Daggerheart rule

When the party works together on one task, one character leads and makes the action roll. Everyone else makes a reaction roll; each success gives the leader +1, and each failure gives −1.

See Group Action Rolls

Gungan Basic

Slang & languages

The Gungans' dialect of Basic, which most Basic speakers can mostly follow.

See Galactic Languages

H

Healing a Crystal

Kyberheart rule

A downtime project to cleanse a bled kyber crystal, which then glows white. A character with Darkness tokens can’t make progress on it.

See Healing a Bled Crystal

Help an Ally

Daggerheart rule

Spend a Hope to describe how you help another character. They roll an advantage die (d6) and add it to their roll.

See Advantage & Disadvantage

Hidden

Daggerheart rule

A condition: when you’re out of sight and others don’t know where you are, rolls against you have disadvantage. It ends when you’re seen or you attack.

See Hidden

Hit Points

Daggerheart rule

How much harm a character can take. Damage marks 1 to 3 Hit Points depending on thresholds. When a PC marks their last one, they make a death move.

See Hit Points & Damage Thresholds

Holocron

Star Wars

A crystal or geometric device that stores the teachings of a Jedi or Sith, opened only through the Force.

HoloNet

Star Wars

The galaxy-wide communication network, carrying news, messages, and holo-broadcasts.

Hope

Daggerheart rule

The players’ resource, up to 6 each. You gain a Hope when you roll with Hope, and spend it on Experiences, helping allies, Tag Team Rolls, and your class’s Hope feature.

See Hope

Hope Feature

Daggerheart rule

A powerful ability each class can use by spending 3 Hope, like the Scoundrel’s Never Tell Me the Odds.

See Classes

Hull

Kyberheart rule

A starship’s Hit Points, marked by damage severity just like a character’s.

See The Starship Sheet

Hutt

Star Wars

A species of huge, slug-like beings, many of whom run criminal empires from the Outer Rim, like Jabba the Hutt.

See Hutt Crime Lord

Huttese

Slang & languages

The language of the Hutts and much of the Outer Rim underworld.

Hyperdrive Class

Kyberheart rule

How fast a ship crosses hyperspace: the lower the class, the faster. Class 1 or 2 is typical; the Millennium Falcon’s Class 0.5 is legendary.

See Hyperdrive Class

Hyperspace

Star Wars

A dimension ships enter to travel faster than light between star systems. Jumping without careful calculation risks flying into a star.

See Hyperdrive Class

I

Imperial Heat

Kyberheart rule

In The Dark Times, a shared track from 0 to 6 measuring how much attention the Empire is paying the party. The GM gains Fear at the start of each session from it, and at 3 or more the party is Wanted.

See Imperial Heat

Imperial Security Bureau (ISB)

Star Wars

The Empire’s intelligence and secret police, hunting rebels and dissidents.

See ISB Agent

Inquisitor

Star Wars

A dark side warrior of the Inquisitorius, often a former Jedi, who hunted surviving Jedi after Order 66. Inquisitors use spinning, double-bladed red lightsabers.

See Inquisitor

Ionized

Kyberheart rule

A temporary condition for a droid, vehicle, or ship that marks its last Stress from an ion attack. It can't use reactions or take other actions until it clears the condition.

See Ionized

J

Jawaese

Slang & languages

The fast, chattering language of the Jawas, which mixes speech with scents.

See Jawa

Jedi

Star Wars

Guardians of peace and justice who follow the light side of the Force and wield lightsabers. Nearly all were killed in the Jedi Purge.

See Force Adept

Jedi Purge

Star Wars

The Empire’s campaign to wipe out the Jedi after Order 66, carried out by clone troopers, Darth Vader, and the Inquisitors.

See The Jedi Purge and the Inquisitorius

K

Knocked Out

Kyberheart rule

What happens to a target that runs out of Stress from a stun attack. Adversaries are defeated without being killed; PCs drop unconscious without making a death move.

See Knocked Out

Kriff / Kriffing

Slang & languages

A common curse across the galaxy.

Kyber Crystal

Star Wars

A Force-attuned crystal at the heart of every lightsaber. Kyber also powers the Death Star’s superlaser, which is why the Empire mined it.

See Kyber Crystals and Lightsabers

L

Laserbrain

Slang & languages

An insult for someone acting foolishly.

Leveling Up

Daggerheart rule

Each new level: take any tier achievement, choose two advancements, add 1 to your damage thresholds, and take a new class card.

See Leveling Up

Lightsaber

Star Wars

A blade of plasma focused through a kyber crystal, the weapon of the Jedi and the Sith.

See Kyber Crystals and Lightsabers

Loadout

Daggerheart rule

The class cards you have active, up to five. Cards you know but haven’t loaded wait in your vault.

See Step 8: Choose Class Cards

M

Magic Damage

Daggerheart rule

One of the two damage types, alongside physical. In Kyberheart, only the Force deals magic damage.

See The Force and Damage Types

Mandalorians

Star Wars

Warriors from Mandalore, organized into clans and known for their beskar armor, jetpacks, and helmets.

See Mandalorian Covert

Mando’a

Slang & languages

The language of the Mandalorians.

Mand’alor

Slang & languages

Mando’a for the ruler of Mandalore, the one who unites the clans.

Mid Rim

Star Wars

The band of worlds between the Core and the Outer Rim.

Minion

Daggerheart rule

An adversary role for rank-and-file foes. A Minion is defeated by any damage, and its Minion (X) feature lets one attack take down extras. Minions are bought in groups the size of the party.

Moff

Moisture Farmer

Star Wars

A farmer on a desert world, like Tatooine, who pulls water from the air with vaporators.

Multiclassing

Daggerheart rule

An advancement available from level 5 that uses both advancements in a level. You gain one class feature and one subclass foundation from a second class, and can take its cards at up to half your level.

N

Nerf Herder

Slang & languages

An insult: someone who herds nerfs (smelly livestock) for a living. Leia called Han one.

O

Offline

When a droid companion marks its last Stress, it goes Offline and leaves the scene. It comes back at your next long rest, or sooner if someone repairs it.

Order 66

Star Wars

The command that turned the clone troopers against their Jedi generals at the end of the Clone Wars (19 BBY).

Outer Rim

Star Wars

The lawless frontier at the galaxy’s edge, home to smugglers, Hutts, and worlds like Tatooine.

P

Parsec

Star Wars

A unit of distance, not time. Han Solo bragged about making the Kessel Run in under 12 parsecs by finding a shorter route.

Proficiency

Daggerheart rule

How many damage dice you roll with weapons. It starts at 1 and rises at levels 2, 5, and 8, and with advancements.

Protocol Droid

Star Wars

A humanoid droid built for etiquette and translation, like C-3PO.

Q

Quirk

Kyberheart rule

A droid companion’s personality trait, like Worrier, Skittish, or Cantankerous, inspired by famous canon droids.

Range

Daggerheart rule

Distances in play: Melee (in reach), Very Close (a few steps), Close (across a small room), Far (across a large room or a street), and Very Far (as far as you can see clearly). Out of range means you can’t target it.

See Maps, Range, and Movement

Reaction Roll

Daggerheart rule

A roll to avoid or resist something, like dodging an explosion. Reaction rolls don’t give the players Hope or the GM Fear.

See Reaction Rolls

Rebel Alliance

Star Wars

The Alliance to Restore the Republic, formed from scattered rebel cells to fight the Empire.

See Rebel Cell

Recall Cost

Daggerheart rule

The Stress you mark to move a card from your vault into your loadout.

See Step 8: Choose Class Cards

Relentless

Daggerheart rule

An adversary feature: Relentless (X) lets the GM spotlight it up to X times in one GM turn, spending Fear each time as usual.

Resistance

Daggerheart rule

Resistance halves damage of a type before thresholds; immunity ignores it. Direct damage can’t be reduced by marking Armor Slots.

See Resistance, Immunity, and Direct Damage

Rest

Daggerheart rule

A short rest takes about an hour and lets you choose two downtime moves; a long rest is a night’s sleep or more, with stronger moves. After three short rests, the next rest must be a long rest.

See Resting and Downtime Moves

Restrained

Daggerheart rule

A condition: you can’t move, but you can still act if you don’t need to move to do it.

See Restrained

Restraining Bolt

Star Wars

A device fixed to a droid to keep it from wandering off or disobeying.

Rodese

Slang & languages

The language of the Rodians.

See Galactic Languages

S

Sabacc

Star Wars

A card game played in cantinas across the galaxy. Han Solo won the Millennium Falcon in a game of it. See Sabacc for the rules.

Scale

Kyberheart rule

A ship or vehicle’s size class: Personal (0), Fighter (1), Freighter (2), or Capital (3). Attacking up or down in scale lowers or raises damage severity by one threshold per step.

See Scale

Scar

Daggerheart rule

A lasting mark from a brush with death (or, in The Dark Times, from falling to the dark side). Each scar permanently crosses out one of your Hope slots.

See Death

Separatists

Star Wars

The Confederacy of Independent Systems, which broke from the Republic and fought the Clone Wars with battle droid armies.

Shield Slots

Kyberheart rule

A starship’s version of Armor Slots: mark one to reduce incoming damage by one threshold.

See The Starship Sheet

Shyriiwook

Slang & languages

The language of the Wookiees, made of growls, roars, and howls that most humans understand but can’t speak.

See Wookiee

Sith

Galactic Timeline

Galactic dates count from the Battle of Yavin: BBY means before it and ABY means after. The Dark Times campaign frame runs from Order 66 (19 BBY) to the Battle of Endor (4 ABY), marked below.

  1. 32 BBY
    The Invasion of Naboo

    The Trade Federation blockades Naboo, and Senator Palpatine rises to Supreme Chancellor.

    The Phantom Menace
  2. 22 BBY
    The Clone Wars begin

    The Battle of Geonosis pits the Republic’s new clone army against the Separatist droid armies.

    Attack of the Clones
  3. 22–19 BBY
    The Clone Wars

    Jedi generals lead clone troopers across the galaxy, while the war wears down the Republic.

    The Clone Wars
  4. 19 BBY
    Order 66 and the Empire

    The clones turn on the Jedi, and Palpatine declares himself Emperor. The Dark Times begin.

    Revenge of the Sith · The Bad Batch
  5. 14 BBY
    Hunted Jedi

    Survivors like Cal Kestis hide in the shadows while Inquisitors hunt them down.

    Jedi: Fallen Order
  6. 13–10 BBY
    The underworld years

    Han Solo flies the Kessel Run as crime syndicates thrive under the Empire.

    Solo
  7. 9 BBY
    Kenobi on Tatooine

    Obi-Wan Kenobi leaves exile to rescue a young Leia Organa.

    Obi-Wan Kenobi · Jedi: Survivor
  8. 5 BBY
    The first sparks

    Cassian Andor’s path to rebellion begins on Ferrix, and the Ghost crew fights the Empire on Lothal.

    Andor · Rebels
  9. 2 BBY
    The Rebel Alliance

    Rebel cells unite into the Alliance to Restore the Republic after the Ghorman Massacre.

    Andor · Rebels
  10. 0 BBY
    Scarif and Yavin

    Rebels steal the Death Star plans on Scarif, and Luke Skywalker destroys the Death Star at Yavin.

    Rogue One · A New Hope
  11. 3 ABY
    Hoth and Bespin

    The Empire routs the Rebels on Hoth, and Han Solo is frozen in carbonite on Bespin.

    The Empire Strikes Back
  12. 4 ABY
    The Battle of Endor

    The second Death Star is destroyed and the Emperor falls. The Dark Times end.

    Return of the Jedi
  13. 5 ABY
    The New Republic

    The Battle of Jakku ends the Galactic Civil War.

  14. 9–11 ABY
    The Outer Rim after the war

    A Mandalorian bounty hunter protects a Force-sensitive foundling while Imperial remnants regroup.

    The Mandalorian · The Book of Boba Fett · Ahsoka

      How the math works

      Start with (3 × the number of PCs) + 2 Battle Points. Adjust: −1 for an easier or shorter fight, −2 if you're using 2 or more Solo adversaries, −2 if you add +1d4 to all adversaries' damage, +1 if you choose an adversary from a lower tier, +1 if you don't include any Bruisers, Hordes, Leaders, or Solos, and +2 for a harder or longer fight.

      Costs: 1 for each group of Minions equal to the party's size, 1 for each Social or Support, 2 for each Horde, Ranged, Skulk, or Standard, 3 for each Leader, 4 for each Bruiser, and 5 for each Solo. The builder applies the roster-based adjustments for you as you add adversaries.

      Tool

      Sabacc

      sabacc

      The galaxy’s favorite way to lose a ship. Three canon ways to play, every card drawn right here, and a hand checker that names what you’re holding.

      Every version is a race toward a target number. Get there exactly and you have sabacc. Miss, and the hand closest to the target wins. That’s called nulrhek.

      To use sabacc in a scene, including stakes, reading the table, and cheating, see Sabacc in Kyberheart Mechanics.

      As seen in Solo: A Star Wars Story and sold at the Toydarian Toymaker in Black Spire Outpost on Batuu (Galaxy’s Edge). Han won the Millennium Falcon from Lando playing this game.

      Goal

      After three rounds, have the hand that totals closest to zero. A hand of exactly zero is a sabacc and also wins the sabacc pot.

      What you need

      • The 62-card deck. Three suits, called staves: circles, triangles, and squares. Each stave has twenty cards: green +1 to +10 and red −1 to −10. Two sylops are worth 0 and belong to no stave. “Sylop” is Old Corellian for “idiot.”
      • Two spike dice. Any two matching six-sided dice work.
      • Chips. 2 to 8 players. Two pots: the hand pot, won every game, and the sabacc pot, won only with a sabacc.

      How to play

      1. Ante and deal. Everyone antes into both pots. Deal each player 2 cards face down. Turn the top card of the draw pile face up to start the discard pile.
      2. Card phase. Starting left of the dealer, each player takes one action:
        • Gain: draw the top card of the draw pile. Keep it, or discard it or another card.
        • Swap: take the top card of the discard pile and discard one of yours in its place.
        • Stand: keep your hand.
        • Junk: fold. Your cards go face up on the discard pile and you’re out until the next game.
      3. Betting phase. Bet, call, raise, or junk, like any card game.
      4. Spike dice phase. The dealer rolls both dice. On doubles, a Sabacc Shift happens: every player discards their whole hand and is dealt the same number of new cards. A great hand can vanish, and a terrible one can be saved.
      5. Repeat. Play three rounds of steps 2 to 4.
      6. Reveal. Everyone left shows their hand. The best hand wins the hand pot. If that hand totals exactly zero, it takes the sabacc pot too. Otherwise the sabacc pot carries over to the next game.

      Winning hands

      These are the Batuu rules, best hand first. Every named hand must total zero. If two players have the same named hand, the one whose pair, set, or run is closest to zero wins (three 4s beat three 5s).

      HandWhat it takesExample
      Pure SabaccExactly two sylops
      Full SabaccTwo +10s, two −10s, and a sylop
      FleetFour of a kind (not 10s) and a sylop
      Yee-HaaOne pair and a sylop
      RhyletThree of a kind of one sign and a pair of the other
      SquadronFour of a kind
      Gee Whiz+1, +2, +3, +4 and a −10 (or the same with the signs flipped)
      Straight KhyronA run of four in a row, any signs
      Bantha’s WildThree of a kind
      Rule of TwoTwo pairs
      Sabacc (one pair)One pair
      SabaccAny other hand that totals zero
      NulrhekNo zero at the table: the closest total wins

      Breaking other ties. For a plain sabacc or a nulrhek, compare these in order: a positive total beats a negative one, then the hand with more cards wins, then the higher total of positive cards, then the highest single positive card. If it’s still tied, each tied player draws one card. The card closest to zero wins, and positive wins ties. Repeat until someone wins. This last step is the Single Blind Draw.

      House rules seen across the galaxy

      Yarith Bespin house rules
      The casino version from the Solo era. After the first bet, each player gets a third card face up, the spike card. Each round you may buy a card for 2 credits and swap it for any card in your hand, including the spike card. Matching dice make everyone replace 2 cards. Double spikes replace all three. The best hand here is the Idiot’s Array (a sylop, +2, and +3). Next is the Prime Sabacc (+10, −10, and a sylop).
      Spike only on double 1s
      Only double 1s cause a Sabacc Shift. Other doubles do nothing. Use this for fewer shifts.
      Straight sabacc
      No dice phase at all. Pure skill and bluffing.
      Market rules
      Gaining or swapping costs a chip into the hand pot, so every draw is a bet.
      Exact hands
      A named hand must contain only its own cards, with no extras.

      The deck and hand checker

      Tap cards to build a hand and see what it is. Tap a card in your hand to put it back.

      The fast version played in the Sublight Lounge aboard the Halcyon (Galaxy’s Edge’s Galactic Starcruiser) and in Black Spire Outpost. It uses the same 62-card deck as Corellian Spike, with no hand rankings.

      Goal

      Choose cards from your hand that total as close as possible to the target number rolled on the gold die. You don’t have to use every card.

      What you need

      • The 62-card deck, the same one Corellian Spike uses.
      • The gold die, which sets the target number. Its faces are 0, 0, +5, −5, +10, and −10.
      • The silver die, which sets the target suit. Its faces show each stave twice: circle, triangle, square.
      • Chips. 2 to 7 players.

      How to play

      1. Ante and roll. Everyone antes. The dealer rolls both dice: the gold die is the target number, and the silver die is the target suit.
      2. Deal. Each player gets 5 cards.
      3. Select. Choose the cards you want to keep and set them face down in front of you. That’s your selection. Then bet.
      4. Shift. Discard every card you didn’t select. The dealer deals you back up to 5 cards.
      5. Improve. Add any of your new cards to your selection and discard the rest. Bet one last time.
      6. Reveal. Everyone shows their selection. The total closest to the target number wins the pot.

      Ways to win

      • Sabacc: your selection hits the target number exactly.
      • Closest wins: if nobody hits it, the closest total takes the pot.
      • Ties: the player with the most cards of the target suit wins. Under the Halcyon tournament rules, sylops count as any suit.
      • The game: pass the deal to the left. Once everyone has dealt once, the player with the most chips wins.

      The deck and selection checker

      Roll a target, then tap cards to build a selection and see how close you are.

      The version played in the Outer Rim cantinas of Star Wars Outlaws, set between The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. You only ever hold two cards, and losing costs you chips.

      Goal

      Hold a Sand card and a Blood card of the same value. The lower the pair, the better. The last player with chips wins the game.

      What you need

      • Two 22-card decks, Sand and Blood. Each deck has three copies of 1 through 6, three Impostors, and one Sylop.
      • Two six-sided dice to roll Impostor values.
      • Chips. Everyone starts with the same number, usually 6 to 8. 2 to 4 players.
      • Shift tokens (optional). Each player brings three.

      How to play

      1. Deal. Shuffle the decks separately. Each player gets one Sand card and one Blood card face down. Turn the top card of each deck face up to start a Sand discard pile and a Blood discard pile.
      2. Turns. On your turn, either:
        • Draw: pay 1 chip and set it in front of you. Take a card from either deck or the top of either discard pile. Then discard one card of that family, either the one you drew or the one you had. You always end with one Sand and one Blood card.
        • Stand: do nothing. It’s free.
      3. Three turns each. After everyone has had three turns, reveal.
      4. Reveal. Roll the two dice for each Impostor and choose one of the two numbers as its value. A Sylop copies the value of your other card. Your hand’s value is the difference between your two cards.
      5. Pay up. The winner takes back every chip they spent this round. Every other player loses the chips they spent. On top of that, a loser with a sabacc pays 1 more chip, and a loser without one pays chips equal to their hand’s difference. A player with no chips is out.

      Winning hands

      HandWhat it takesExample
      Pure SabaccTwo Sylops. Unbeatable.
      Prime SabaccA pair of 1s
      SabaccAny other pair. Lower beats higher, so 2s beat 6s.
      Sylop SabaccA Sylop with any card. It ranks the same as a real pair of that card.
      NulrhekNo pair. The smallest difference wins, then the lower cards.

      Shift tokens

      Each player brings three shift tokens to the table. You can play one at the start of your turn, and each token can be used only once per game. These are adapted from Outlaws for tabletop play.

      Free DrawDraw this turn without paying.
      RefundTake back 2 of the chips you’ve spent.
      Extra RefundTake back 3 of the chips you’ve spent.
      General TariffEvery other player pays 1 chip.
      Target TariffOne player you choose pays 2 chips.
      EmbargoThe next player must stand.
      ImmunityOther players’ tokens can’t affect you until the reveal.
      MarkdownSylops are worth 0 this round.
      Major FraudImpostors are worth 6 this round.
      Cook the BooksSabacc rankings flip this round, so high pairs beat low ones.
      Prime SabaccRoll the dice and pick a number. A pair of that number is the best sabacc this round.
      EmbezzlementTake 1 chip from every other player.
      General AuditEvery player who stands pays 2 chips.
      Target AuditOne player you choose pays 3 chips if they stand.
      ExhaustionOne player you choose discards their hand and draws a new one.
      Direct TransactionTrade hands with a player you choose.

      The decks and hand checker

      Tap one Sand card and one Blood card. Impostors roll their dice for you, and the checker picks the better number.
